#132846. Cycling Taught Me How to Suffer—a Lesson That Helped Me Lose 140 Pounds and Find Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1788 w)
📖 Baca

Cycling Taught Me How to Suffer—a Lesson That Helped Me Lose 140 Pounds and Find Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that SEPTEMBER 2026, THE week of the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal and the city was lousy with bicycles.
  • Industry observers note that I'd heard elite cyclists—guys like Toms Skujins, Sean Quinn, and Mike Woods—talk about this pain in passing, but I was in Montreal to learn more.
  • Industry observers note that IN 2001, I was an obese drug addict.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that SEPTEMBER 2026, THE week of the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal and the city was lousy with bicycles. On most corners, a new pack of amateur cyclists gathered. Bixi—Montreal’s bike share program—was represented, but as a garnish to the inundation of mountain, beach, fixie, and road bikes, along with their riders from around the world, taking over the city. I watched all this in awe. Cycling changed me because it taught me how to suffer. The sport familiarized me with the type of suffering that wrecks you, but you put yourself through it on purpose. You suffer to emerge resilient and better.

Industry observers note that I'd heard elite cyclists—guys like Toms Skujins, Sean Quinn, and Mike Woods—talk about this pain in passing, but I was in Montreal to learn more. I wanted to know if they saw the power of suffering in the same way I did.

Industry observers note that IN 2001, I was an obese drug addict. Checking into rehab that year put a number to my weight: 536 pounds. I’d been diagnosed with congestive heart failure, drugs were promptly killing me, and I was motivated to change. Once I’d been sober for a year, I was able to see that my weight was causing me suffering.

It has been revealed that standing was a herculean effort, placing my feet in the right spot to support me, calculating the angle my knees would be in at the apex of my shifting mass, deep breath, locked core, and a hope and a prayer that I didn’t topple. Tying my shoes was done in bursts of held breath and near-blackouts. I slept sitting up, because the pressure of my chest caused me to choke and gasp. I could once soothe that suffering with food and drugs and kick that discomfort down the road a bit, but in sobriety I needed healthy outlets.

I’d successfully managed lose 100 pounds before my wife tricked me into going to the gym. When she’d ask that I go, I’d tell her that the gym was a place for fit people. So she bought me a package with a personal trainer, said I could flake on the appointments, but I’d be flushing money down the toilet if I did. I went, but I was geared towards avoidance, and whenever something in the gym got hard, I’d just tell the trainer I couldn’t do it.

According to recent reports, riding a bike was something I did during outings with my wife and little kids maybe a few times a year. We’d cram our minivan full of bikes, find the flattest part of the Venice bike path, and slowly cruise for ten minutes at a time. Getting them back into the car was the hardest thing I had to work through.

Little did I know that someday cycling would be the key to changing my life.

ROUND AND ROUND I went losing and regaining weight. In 2009, after getting down to 300 pounds and ballooning back up to over 400, faced with having to start over once again, I turned my sights to running.

I tried running on a desolate stretch of the LA river near my house in Studio City. Not only was I unbearably slow, running hurt. My flat feet sent electric jolts of white-hot pain cascading up and through my body. That first day, I’d wrapped my ankles so tightly with ace bandages that my toes went numb. My feet were no better off and my nipples bled. The next day I could barely stand. The suffering didn’t stop when I stopped running. My feet, ankles, knees, and hips hurt long after—and I had no control over it.

It has been revealed that with running out, but I turned to an old beach cruiser in our shed. The street we lived on was relatively flat, but every street branching off it was a steep climb. After a few rounds on my street, I decided to be ballsy and see how long I could last going uphill.

My legs were screaming, but there was no electric jolt of pain in my pedal stroke. My heart thundered, my mind told me I had to stop. But without the jarring jolt I got when my feet hit the ground while running, I knew I could go further.

According to recent reports, despite never riding my bike uphill as a kid, despite weighing 400 pounds, despite every physical and mental signal in me telling me to quit, I made it up to the top of that hill, up to Mulholland and Laurel Canyon, and it was glorious. Fighting through that urge to stop was incredible; getting to the top even more so. The pain while running was a warning that stayed with me after I stopped. The pain of cycling uphill was legs, lungs, and heart. I could push through it, and it stopped when I stopped.

Industry observers note that I asked Tour de France cyclist Mike Woods about this distinction of suffering when I was in Montreal. “Suffering is a bit of a misnomer for endurance events. Are you really suffering? It’s elected, you know?” he told me. “You choose the pain, you choose when to stop, you choose when to keep going. I don’t truly suffer. Suffering is when you don’t choose for that pain to be inflicted on you”.

In a recent development, and then he said something that really resonated with me: “But it does prepare you for real suffering, when you have something bad happen to you in life. Doing endurance events, I find—it’s fake suffering, but when you have those bad moments in your life, you’re better prepared to manage them.”.

Recent findings suggest that AFTER THAT HILL climb, I started riding my bike regularly, eventually graduated to a mountain bike, and then to a road bike. I rode to the top of every mountain in Los Angeles. I discovered I was capable of so much more than my mind or body allowed me to believe. Legs screaming, heart pounding, mind numbing, this was suffering, and I found that I loved it. And, like Woods said, I found that the more I suffered on a bicycle, the less I suffered off it.

Sources indicate that “One day at a time, one pedal stroke at a time. Just move forward,” Toms Skujins, a two-time Latvian road race champion, told me in Montreal. “When you’re racing, you can stop at any point. You’re the one doing the damage, you know? That’s very voluntary suffering, because there’s, obviously, things in the world that happen where you don’t choose to suffer, and you have no choice there. Here… if your legs are screaming too much, you can just stop. For me, that kind of suffering is definitely easier to take.”.

Within my first year of cycling, I was riding every day. There was a loop that took me from Studio City over the hill to West Hollywood. I’d cross Los Angeles, ride up PCH, cross the Santa Monica Mountains, and ride back to Studio City along Ventura Boulevard. It got me 100 miles and 8,000 feet of climbing, and I did it a few times a week. I’d do shorter 30- to 50-mile rides on the remaining days.

Sean Quinn, a US pro cyclist, gets it: “It sounds easy when you’re sitting on the couch, but when you’re actually in that moment suffering, your body’s basically sending you all the signals it can to make you just do anything else, just stop, stop the suffering,” he told me. “There’s no instant fix to a lot of your suffering. You have to be patient, accept that it’s gonna be shitty for a while, and wait it out, and keep a cool head, and eventually it does get better. Of course, you have to take action.”.

When I was riding every day, I got down to 213 pounds. I’d like to say I stayed there. But I went back to work, stopped riding, my diet unraveled, and over the next few years, I gained nearly all of it back.

In 2016, 400 pounds again, I ruptured the biceps tendon in my right arm and had to have surgery to repair it. As a sober guy, I turned down the post-op painkillers. I was up all night in pain and had to work the following day. On set, with the motion of production buzzing around me, the pain was dull, but it was unrelenting, just like a ride up Angeles Crest Highway, more than 120 miles out-and-back, with over 13,000 feet of elevation gain. I hadn’t chosen the injury, but I had chosen to go without the pills, and that reminded me of the pain on the bike, something I picked and something I knew would come to an end. I’d remind myself of that and go back to learning my lines and preparing for the scene.

That day reminded me that I knew how to do this. So I got back on a diet, and by 2018 I was down to 260, and I’ve held steady there ever since.

In a recent development, riding a bike taught me that I could suffer now in benefit of tomorrow. It’s been the most powerful lesson I’ve learned about myself.

It has been revealed that ON THE DAY of the elite men’s road race, we fans lined the streets. There was dedicated bike parking near the finish line—Fans Village Bonjour Montreal—with thousands of bikes in neat rows. We all lined up to watch the attacks, riders going solo for that long and treacherous circuit. An American, Brandon McNulty, went off the front with about three laps to go and won the World Championship this year. It was thrilling to see. At the press conference afterward he said, “I was just dying, but I kept pushing.”.

Industry observers note that leaving Canada, I couldn’t help but think that I shared something with everyone else there for the races. A secret membership, dues paid in sweat, and a code, to respect and revel in my voluntary suffering.

I’d gone to Montreal to ask the riders if they saw suffering the way I did, and in different words, all three told me that what you do on the bike carries over into the rest of your life. I’d thought cycling taught me how to suffer, but what it did was give me a place where I was in control of it, where I could make it a practice, so that when the suffering of life came along, the suffering I had no control over, I was better equipped to deal with it.

Hyundai is shaking up its 2027 electric vehicle lineup: Here’s what’s changing

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the newly introduced IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.
  • Hyundai confirmed its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the upcoming IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.
  • While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the newly introduced IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.

Hyundai confirmed its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the upcoming IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.

While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.

In a recent development, the IONIQ 6 N is Hyundai’s second performance EV, following the IONIQ 5 N. Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric sports car delivers a combined 641 hp and 568 lb-ft of torque.

Hyundai mentioned the IONIQ 6 N can sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 3.2 seconds, beating the IONIQ 5 N at 3.25 seconds.

Like the IONIQ 5 N, it also includes fun added features, like N e-Shift and an N Active Sound+ system that simulates the sounds and sensations of a traditional gas-powered sports car with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission.

It has been revealed that it uses an 84 kWh battery that provides up to 245 miles of pure electric driving range. Thanks to its 800V ultra-fast charging architecture, the IONIQ 6 N can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Like Hyundai’s other electric vehicles, it comes standard with a native NACS charging port and a CCS adapter.

The 2027 IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are mostly carryover models with a few minor changes, while the IONIQ 5 N remains the same as the 2026 model year.

Changes to the IONIQ 5 for the 2027 model year include roof rails, which are now available on the SEL trim and above; previously, they were only available on the XRT and Limited trims.

Hyundai HomeLink will be available exclusively on the Limited trim, rather than SEL and above, in the current 2026 model year, while the Cargo Cover will be offered as an Accessory only.

Regarding color options, the Gravity Gold Matte and Sage Silver Matte will no longer be available for the 2027 IONIQ 5.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250, making it one of the most affordable EVs in the US.

That’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. The extended-range SE RWD model is $2,500 more, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Hyundai’s three-row SUV also received a handful of updates. The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 9 will be available with a fresh Calligraphy Black Ink trim, while the Calligraphy Design will no longer be offered.

Recent findings suggest that the 2027 IONIQ 9 Calligraphy and Calligraphy Black Ink trims gain a Virtual Gear Shift and heated third-row seats. All variants also gain a Tailgate Emergency Lamp.

According to recent reports, on the one hand... the Ioniq5 is due for an revision. On the other... I still absolutely love the way it looks, and notice just about every one I pass on the road.

In a recent development, hyundai has yet to announce prices for the 2027 model. The base 2026 IONIQ 9 S starts at $58,995 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 335 miles.

The previous top-spec Performance Calligraphy Design AWD started at $76,490, so you can expect the upcoming Calligraphy Black Ink to be around the same, if not even more.

#132842. Tesla confirms rare new delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

Tesla confirms rare new delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has confirmed a newly introduced batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s a rare data point.
  • The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, demonstrates four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has confirmed a newly introduced batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a rare data point. Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its new Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.

The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, demonstrates four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.

Hello Windy CityChicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery pic.twitter.com/75kig8yWsb.

But the only 50-truck Semi order tied to Chicago belongs to HMD Trucking. The family-owned carrier was founded in Chicago in 1998, runs more than 650 trucks (almost all diesel), and ordered 50 Semis right after Tesla’s production event in September.

According to recent reports, HMD took its first truck on November 2 and says it’s the first Tesla Semi registered in Illinois. COO Michael Mahler noted Tesla “has been transparent with us regarding the capabilities of Semi every step of the way.”.

Sources indicate that the organization ran a Semi for more than 4,000 miles over the summer and averaged 1.74 kWh per mile, right in line with Tesla’s 1.7 kWh/mile claim. The first trucks will mostly handle local runs around Chicago, and HMD is installing its own chargers there since Tesla’s Megacharger network is still concentrated along the I-5 and I-10 corridors in the West.

Owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend the deal is worth about $15 million. That’s roughly $300,000 per truck, in line with the ~$290,000 Long Range pricing we reported when the first truck came off the high-volume line and a long way from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017.

Here’s the problem: it’s nearly impossible to tell how many Semis Tesla is actually building.

In a recent development, tesla rolled out volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025. It claims the 1.8 million sq ft plant is built for 50,000 trucks a year. But it never gave a ramp schedule, and its quarterly production and delivery reports only count “passenger vehicles sold to customers.” The Semi isn’t in there.

Industry observers note that so we’re left with proxies. Tesla indicates its Semi fleet has over 98% uptime, without saying how major that fleet is. Before this year, the largest Semi fleet was PepsiCo’s, at 86 trucks in 2024. California’s truck voucher program received 965 Semi applications between January 2025 and February 2026, which points to real demand but says nothing about output.

The order book is the other clue. Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks. And now HMD’s 50 are rolling into Chicago, one of the first Semi fleets that will have to deal with a Midwest winter. Wisconsin’s Paper Transport has also been piloting a Semi in the Chicago market since the summer.

None of that adds up to a production rate, but it does look like Tesla is slowly ramping up deliveries.

It has been revealed that tesla keeps the Semi numbers vague on purpose. It’s happy to talk about a 50,000-truck-a-year factory, and it posts hero shots when a batch ships, but it won’t give the one number that shows whether the factory is anywhere close to that.

I think the semi is going to be a big seller but its going to take some time to produce enough of them and for companies to gather enough data. Once the investment is justified, there will be customers and repeat customers. After that, it will only be a matter of time before other electric semi truck manufacturers start popping up with offerings and thats a good thing for everyone.

Industry observers note that the 50,000 figure is what makes the Semi look like a real business to investors instead of a niche program that took nine years to get going. Tesla has a long history of quoting capacity long before it reaches it, so we shouldn’t treat “built for 50,000” as anything more than a ceiling.

Our read: Tesla is still far from that 50,000 rate. Fifty trucks for one customer is 0.1% of a year at full capacity, and if Tesla were shipping in large volumes, a single 50-unit batch wouldn’t get its own post. But the ramp has clearly started, the order book is real, and it’s plausible Tesla gets into the thousands by the end of the year.

Industry observers note that good for HMD, too. A 650-truck diesel fleet in a cold market is exactly the kind of customer the Semi has to win. Malukas admitted “we don’t have real numbers yet” on savings, and HMD’s own blog is fairly sober about cost and winter range. Local routes, depot charging and a Chicago winter is the right way to find out. It all sounds plausible for the Tesla Semi.

#132840. Tesla extends Cybertruck production to late summer 2027 amid fan backlash

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1126 w)

EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla extends Cybertruck production to late summer 2027 amid fan backlash

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk now states Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first announced it was killing it.
  • The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it claims about Tesla’s future as a tech giant that sells cars to people.
  • On November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk now states Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first announced it was killing it.

The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it claims about Tesla’s future as a tech giant that sells cars to people.

On November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab. On November 9, he wrote the line would shut “in about 8 months” and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.” Now it’s the end of summer.

In order to work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog, production will be extended through the end of summer 2027.

Industry observers note that the reasons have moved around just as much. First it was factory space, then “a very limited number of smart, dedicated people,” then the “opportunity cost” of the truck’s complexity. We went through each of them: Tesla is ending the Cybertruck as sales stall at about 10% of strategy, Musk’s demand claim doesn’t survive the numbers, and Musk admitted Tesla doesn’t have the talent to run more than one vehicle program.

According to recent reports, and the “backlog” is one Tesla built itself. Before the announcement, the truck was selling at a pace of roughly 30,000 units a year, about 10% of the 250,000 Tesla planned for, on a line with over 125,000 units of installed capacity. Telling people the truck is going away creates a last-call rush. That’s not demand Tesla was missing before.

According to recent reports, tesla also raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% the same day and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. The cheapest Cybertruck you can order is now $92,490, up from $69,990 in early August.

In a recent development, some of the people in that backlog have been waiting a while. Several cheering in Musk’s replies say they’re still waiting on the $59,990 Cybertruck Tesla sold for “10 days only” in February. One asked whether Tesla will prioritize Premium and Cyberbeast orders over theirs. Musk didn’t answer.

According to recent reports, the most telling replies weren’t about the truck. Chuck Cook, one of the best-known FSD testers in the Tesla community, quote-tweeted Musk asking him to “change your mind,” adding: “Cybercab won’t haul my bees.”.

Another longtime Tesla supporter, Phil Trubey, asked for “a vehicle roadmap post end of summer 2027,” followed by: “Will Tesla make any other vehicle?”.

In a recent development, that’s the right question, and Tesla hasn’t unveiled a single newly introduced consumer vehicle to answer it. Tesla started 2026 with five consumer vehicle programs: Model S, Model X, Model 3, Model Y, and Cybertruck. It ended Model S and Model X production in the spring, citing “autonomy.” The Cybertruck goes next. By fall 2027, Tesla’s consumer lineup will be the Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles that rolled out in 2017 and 2020.

Tesla’s answer to the affordable car it promised for years was stripped-down “Standard” versions of those same two vehicles. In China, its second-biggest market, Tesla turned Giga Shanghai into an export hub, and domestic retail sales crashed 66% in October to the lowest level in over four years.

Industry observers note that even Unplugged Performance, the biggest Tesla tuner around, offered to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands and pay a license fee. People want this truck built. Tesla doesn’t.

We’ve been warning about this for years, and for years we got called haters for it.

It has been revealed that the pattern has been clear since Tesla swapped its affordable car aims for Robotaxi in 2024. No new consumer platform. Model S and X killed “for autonomy.” Cybertruck killed “for Cybercab.” A Roadster pitched as a thruster stunt nine years after its unveiling. Every product decision points away from selling cars to people and toward robotaxis and Optimus, two businesses that don’t generate meaningful revenue today.

I am beginning to suspect that Elon does not always tell the truth.

As long as we have an economic climate that allows massive amounts of money to be made off of speculation as opposed to actual product, future bots and robotaxis have a great deal of value whether they actually become viable or not.

Sources indicate that A two-to-three-month extension doesn’t change any of that. It’s a gesture to the loudest part of the fan base, and it happens to let Tesla sell a few thousand more trucks at prices up to 10% higher than last week. Fine. But the people who bought into Tesla’s mission to accelerate the world’s transition to sustainable energy are now realizing that mission was quietly rewritten, and the word “sustainable” didn’t make the cut.

Tesla is becoming a tech giant that sells two aging EVs to fund a bet on autonomy. That might work out for shareholders. We have our doubts, given Tesla is still behind Waymo by every public metric. But it’s a lot less exciting for the people who wanted the next great Tesla car.

The question for fans now: when the Model 3 and Model Y get their own “opportunity cost” post on X, will anyone actually be surprised?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its new full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.
  • The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.
  • Recent findings suggest that after opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD said the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its new full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.

The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.

Recent findings suggest that after opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD said the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours. Two weeks later, preorders reached over 100,000.

By the time it went on sale in mid-June, over 150,000 buyers had preordered the Great Tang, marking a latest record for a single BYD model.

While it has been the top-selling pure electric large SUV for two months, with more than 10,000 sold since it hit the market, BYD issued an apology on November 11 for fitting the wrong front and rear wheel rims on some Great Tang models.

The apology comes after several owners complained that the wheels were improperly installed on their vehicles.

BYD said the glitch stemmed from a coding error by the wheel mesh assembly supplier, which led to incorrect assembly on some Great Tang vehicles.

The company remarked it “immediately” released an investigation and corrected the matter so newly built vehicles will not be affected. In addition, the supplier introduced a new visual error-prevention mechanism to limit issues like this going forward.

BYD said the glitch does not affect the vehicle’s handling or pose a safety risk during driving.

The organization stated owners can take affected vehicles to their local service center for a free inspection and professional wheel rim replacement. It’s also offering a replacement vehicle or compensation for transportation expenses.

Effective immediately, BYD mentioned, the warranty on affected Great Tang vehicles will also be restarted.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest Premium EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500).

According to recent reports, all versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries. While the base Premium model uses a 105.79 kWh battery, the Flagship EV trim uses a larger 130.15 kWh battery that delivers up to 590 miles (950 km) of CLTC range. It starts at 269,900 yuan ($40,000).

The Great Tang is huge, measuring 5,263 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,800 mm high, with a wheelbase of 3,130 mm.

Industry observers note that in comparison, that’s bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9. It’s closer in size to the Li Auto L9.

Based on a 1,000V architecture with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric SUV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

After launching in China, BYD executive vice president Stella Li mentioned the flagship SUV will go on sale in Europe and other overseas markets by the end of 2026 or early 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kia became the first non-European brand to score a hat trick at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, Germany’s most prestigious auto awards.

The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.

This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.

The award is organized by AUTO BILD and BILD am SONNTAG with 90 newly introduced models nominated this year. Readers chose 27 finalists, three in each of the nine classes, which were then tested by a panel of celebrities and auto experts.

Sources indicate that the judges tested the vehicles at the DEKRA-Lausitzring racetrack. Vehicles were judged on handling, comfort, ease of use, quality, and everyday practicality, as well as the sustainability and value they offer.

Kia won across three very different categories with the fully electric EV2 and EV5, alongside the gas-powered K4 Sportswagon.

The EV2, Kia’s entry-level electric SUV, won the award for the “Best Car Under €30,000.” Developed specifically for Europe, the compact EV is only 4.06 meters long, but offers up to 403 liters of cargo space.

It also offers a WLTP driving range of up to 453 km (281 miles), which is among the longest in its class.

Kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Launched in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.

According to recent reports, it’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).

Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, released in May, outperformed the upcoming Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.

In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.

Recent findings suggest that sadly, Kia has no plans to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 (see our review) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”.

Industry observers note that the 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.

The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

#132831. The Science Behind Mogging

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1513 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

The Science Behind Mogging

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that AT SIX-FOOT-FOUR, I’m not accustomed to feeling physically dwarfed.
  • Industry observers note that until recently, I didn’t have a name for this peculiar, perhaps Palaeolithic phenomenon.
  • “To mog” entered the lexicon thanks to figures like Braden Peters, better known as Clavicular.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that AT SIX-FOOT-FOUR, I’m not accustomed to feeling physically dwarfed. Sure, I might not have bulging muscles—but I confess I occasionally survey the other men in the gym and entertain the idea that I might be the hottest guy in the room. Sometimes, though, a bigger, better looking dude walks in and starts lifting heavier weights than me. My confidence evaporates, along with, I imagine, the admiring glances of all the men and women (who, on reflection, might not actually have been paying me any mind).

Industry observers note that until recently, I didn’t have a name for this peculiar, perhaps Palaeolithic phenomenon. Mogging, derived from “alpha Male Of the Group,” describes the act of one man outshining another, through any combination of height, muscularity, facial attractiveness, status, or charisma (a.k.a. “aura”). On the receiving end, it’s the sudden, visceral realization that another man might be stronger or better-looking than you, and the cascade of feelings of inferiority that follow.

“To mog” entered the lexicon thanks to figures like Braden Peters, better known as Clavicular. The 20-year-old looksmaxxing influencer was spectacularly “frame-mogged” on his own livestream in a viral moment earlier this year. The curious phrasing captured online attention, and on November 3 “mogging” was crowned Collins Dictionary’s word of the year for 2026.

Recent findings suggest that but this type of social scenario didn’t just emerge with the dawn of the internet. I was curious: Does this emasculating sensation stem from an ancient status instinct, an ego threat, a form of social comparison, or something else? And why are some men so sensitive to it?

According to recent reports, THIS CONCERN OF mogging raises a question: Why should another man’s stature have such an immediate effect on my self-esteem? It’s a theme explored in the classics. In Homer’s Iliad, the ancient Greek epic, King Priam spots the enormous warrior Ajax, “whose head and shoulders tower above the rest.” Yet Homer also understood that size wasn't everything. Earlier in the same passage, Menelaus is described as broader-shouldered than Odysseus, the cunning hero played by Matt Damon in The Odyssey—but the shorter man’s extraordinary eloquence renders his stature irrelevant.

Modern researchers have also looked for answers. Human judgment “is by nature comparative” and social comparisons are “spontaneous, effortless, and unintentional reactions to the performance of others,” according to a 2014 review of the early indications on the brain mechanisms of social comparison and their influence on the reward system.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, other related research found that physically stronger men were perceived as having higher social status, partly because they were considered more capable leaders. But does this make the discomfort of being mogged inevitable?

Psychologists distinguish between dominance, in which status is secured through intimidation, and prestige, which is earned through the admiration of others. Research suggests that even if the strongest and most attractive may initially draw outsized attention, or mog, prestige is ultimately conferred upon those who benefit the group, rather than pursue aggressive self-interest.

For couples therapist Sarah Tilley, this dynamic reflects the tension between our instinctive deference to appearances and our recognition of its limitations. Snap judgments of competence from candidates’ faces predicted almost 69 percent of US senate races in 2004, according to a study in Science,.

Recent findings suggest that “There is a deference to beauty and we’re all culprits,” she indicates. “Beauty trumps intelligence, but only for a short amount of time. Smart people will know that, but it takes wisdom.” In other words, the actual effects of a mog could be fleeting if there is someone smarter in the room.

In a recent development, WHAT IS ACTUALLY happening when you feel the mog? Turns out, there are chemical responses behind those feelings of self-doubt.

“A review of more than 200 lab studies found that our cortisol is reliably spiked when we feel that others are judging us and when we can’t control the outcome,” claims Dr Manesh Girn, a neuroscientist and men’s work facilitator.

“Envy toward someone who outranks you on something you care about also activates the anterior cingulate cortex, a region tied to processing pain and conflict,” he states, citing a study on the neural correlates of envy and schadenfreude (the feeling of satisfaction when someone faces consequences they deserve).

Sources indicate that but the susceptibility to feeling mogged also depends on one’s values and sense of self-worth. “Shorter men are more sensitive than taller men to dominance cues in other men's faces and voices,” adds Girn. In the envy study, pain responses only arose when the other person’s perceived superiority was in a domain the participant particularly cared about.

Recent findings suggest that looksmaxxer-in-chief Peters admitted last month that he now simply removes himself from social settings when there’s a possibility he might be mogged. “It really has a soul-crushing effect,” he told podcaster Patrick Bet-David, recalling a recent weight room encounter. “We just felt the mog from all the way across the gym to the point where I just left. Why would I want that internal pressure?”.

Such an extreme reaction suggests “a maladaptive mindset,” notes Charlotte Markey, a professor of psychology at Rutgers University. “Social comparison is a very normal process, including in terms of our physical attributes.”.

Recent findings suggest that for some men in 2026, that drives an obsession to become the strongest of the pack. This can become genuinely debilitating.

Industry observers note that “I've cared for young people who then go to the gym five plus hours a day, and it starts to detract from their quality of life,” says Jason Nagata, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Francisco, who researches male body image. “The concern is when self-improvement becomes self-worth, because it becomes dependent on outperforming someone else.”.

And while this might be driven by instinct, the experts caution against succumbing to our baser instincts. “It may be evolutionarily baked in,” notes Markey, “but we want to be careful not to oversimplify here. We aren’t cavemen.”.

In a recent development, HOWEVER, THE CAVEMAN is not quite dead. We form impressions of a face within a tenth of a second, and people can estimate a man’s upper body strength from his face alone. For our ancestors, misjudging who could beat them in a fight may have been a costly mistake. Some research suggests that our sensitivity to physical formidability reflects this ancient pressure, which may help explain why strength continues to influence perceptions of status.

Sources indicate that despite sometimes feeling the mog (and after injuries that prevent heavy lifting), I’m generally content to stick to lighter weights in the gym rather than packing on mass to stand out more in a room. Yet I wonder whether my own instinctive competitiveness has affected my relationships with other men. If I’m constantly assessing where I stand in some invisible hierarchy, like a dog jostling for position in its pack, surely it becomes more difficult to strike up friendships.

In a 2017 study of 100 physically active young men, researchers found that those at risk of muscle dysmorphia were less inclined to socialize than their peers, potentially due to social comparison tendencies. The pursuit of the perfect physique, it seems, can come at the expense of the very relationships it might be intended to improve.

SO WHY, AFTER millennia of social comparison, do we have this very modern understanding of the mogging dynamic? Social media has transformed what was once a largely local competition into a global one, exposing men to an endless parade of gorgeous bodies and faces against which to measure themselves (albeit at lower rates than women). “The Greeks didn’t compare themselves with the best, idealized versions of everyone in the world,” says Nagata.

Indeed, researchers effectively recreated the experience of being mogged in a study involving 300 men aged 18 to 30. They were randomly assigned to view images of bare-chested and muscular men alongside clothed photos and pictures of scenery. Exposure to the half-naked Chads resulted in significantly lower body satisfaction.

I would never flee a gym or a bar upon the entrance of a potentially more attractive man. But back in April—shortly after mogging entered my lexicon—I couldn’t help noticing how much attention a very handsome (and very muscular) longtime male friend was receiving. One woman I didn’t even know basically cat-called him on the street and complimented his outfit. Naturally I assessed my own. It wasn’t nearly as cool, I lamented.

According to recent reports, now, after years of feeling this mysterious, disempowering sensation in his tech giant without entirely being able to place it, I had a name for my predicament: I’d been mogged. Still, I was able to keep it together. We enjoyed our lunch, and we remain friends.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps the instinct to compare ourselves is unavoidable. Sometimes I wonder whether the worst thing about discovering mogging is becoming conscious of a competition I never even realized I was in.

Mattha Busby is a journalist who covers drug policy, culture, and health.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD’s fresh EV may be about the size of a Toyota Camry, but it’s playing in a whole different league when it comes to technology.

BYD introduced the second-generation Seal 07 last week, calling it “the fresh choice for a class-leading luxury experience.”.

It’s available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with prices starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.

Both versions measure 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide, and 1,495 mm high, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase, which is slightly longer than the Toyota Camry.

Don’t let the price fool you, however, the vehicle is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough technology.

The newly introduced Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery that provides a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km).

According to recent reports, thanks to the second-gen Blade Batteries and BYD’s Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes.

The Seal 07 is also BYD’s first vehicle to debut with its upcoming Disus-M Intelligent Magnetorheological Body Control System.

It has been revealed that the setup features a front double-wishbone suspension and an enhanced rear five-link suspension. It works alongside BYD’s road-surface sensors that use LiDAR, plus its iTAC 2.0 Intelligent Torque Adaptation System.

Zhang Zhuo, the general manager of BYD’s Ocean sales division, offered a better look at how the system works in real life in the video shown above.

According to recent reports, BYD mentioned the system provides ultra-fast response times down to the millisecond. The advanced suspension system adjusts damping force across a wide range of 100 to 10,000 Nm.

It’s equipped on the all-electric Flagship Seal 07 variant, while lower-priced versions have the Disus-C intelligent body control system. The top-spec EV model with the Disus-M setup starts at 172,900 yuan ($26,000). Still, not too bad for what you get.

Inside, the newly introduced Seal 07 adopts BYD’s new interior design, including a 15.6″ floating center infotainment screen, a 10.25″ instrument cluster, and two rear passenger entertainment screens.

BYD added a few premium extras, including a built-in 6.8L smart refrigerator, zero gravity seats, and driver headrest audio.

Quite impressive for sure. What's more impressive is that GM/Cadillac first offered magnetic ride control back in 2002 (a full 24 years ago!!). It may not have been quite as advanced as this system in 2026, but still one of the most advanced suspension systems offered to date for a line of vehicles.

According to recent reports, I really want this car!! I truly hope BYD will be able to sell this in the USA soon.

Higher-priced versions are available with BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, which includes a roof-mounted LiDAR. The setup provides safety and convenience features like Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking.

The Simple Guide to Finding a Weighted Vest You’ll Actually Use

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Slip on a weighted vest, and suddenly your regular walk, chores, or bodyweight exercises feel a little more rewarding—the extra weight offering a simple boost in effort and making us more aware of the way our bodies maintain balance and stability.
  • According to recent reports, I’m a certified personal trainer, and I sometimes recommend weighted vests to older adult clients as a way to add extra challenge to walking, cardio, and bodyweight exercises.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Slip on a weighted vest, and suddenly your regular walk, chores, or bodyweight exercises feel a little more rewarding—the extra weight offering a simple boost in effort and making us more aware of the way our bodies maintain balance and stability.

According to recent reports, I’m a certified personal trainer, and I sometimes recommend weighted vests to older adult clients as a way to add extra challenge to walking, cardio, and bodyweight exercises. While recent research suggests that weighted vests may not have a dramatic impact on bone density, they’re still a safe and convenient way to increase the load on your muscles and joints, helping you push yourself a little harder than usual.

Weighted vests let you add extra resistance to walking, stair climbing, jumping, push-ups, and pull-ups without needing to grip dumbbells or barbells. Some clients even wear them during everyday activities like cleaning, yard work, or mowing the lawn—making fitness a little more functional and, yes, a bit more fun.

That mentioned, if you’ve been diagnosed with osteoporosis, consult your doctor before adding a weighted vest to your exercise routine, while folks who are pregnant or experience back, neck, or joint pain should also avoid them.

It has been revealed that before you take the plunge on purchasing a weighted vest, you should consider the resistance level, workouts such as walking or HIIT, and whether materials are sweat-resistant to determine which one is best for you. Ready to get vested?

After testing a handful of weighted vests for weeks, the trophy goes to the Omorpho G-Vest for its remarkable comfort, ideal weight, and sleek design. I spent a week wearing it for my regular lifting sessions and hour-long walks. It’s easy to wear for my normal gym routine, which includes moves such as walking lunges, Copenhagen planks, pull-ups, and push-ups.

Sources indicate that however, I found it to be challenging when worn for heavier compound lifts like front squats, deadlifts, and barbell rows. Other than walking lunges, I wouldn’t normally add load to those exercises because of the logistics of holding or hanging weight, but the vest makes it possible to add resistance without gripping anything.

Industry observers note that the fit is another reason the G-Vest earns the top spot. This vest is surprisingly comfortable considering it weighs just over five pounds from stainless steel balls. While the back panels have more weight—226 stainless steel balls on the back and 122 on the front—the weight distribution feels uniform when wearing.

It’s also compact—from the shoulder straps to the bottom of the vest is about 17 inches, which, for me, is great since I have a very short torso. It also doesn't dig into the top of my hip bone when I move around.

According to recent reports, even if you don’t have a short torso, you’ll still appreciate the soft-to-the-touch polyester fabric, despite it feeling like neoprene (synthetic rubber). I use adjustable cords at the sides for a customized fit. There are also straps on the shoulders to accommodate a wider frame, or if you want the vest to sit a little lower on your torso. For reference, I have mine on the shortest setting.

Sources indicate that one downside of the G-Vest is its limited size options. There are only two: S/M or L/XL. I highly recommend using the size chart to determine which fit is best for you. I’m typically a medium when shopping for athletic tops, but I chose the L/XL because my chest circumference is on the cusp of both options. It’s also worth mentioning that the weight of the S/M vest is four pounds and 12 ounces, while the L/XL is five pounds and six ounces.

Read More: Omorpho G-Vest Review.

In a recent development, you can shell out up to $300 for a weighted vest, but not everyone needs all the extra features that come with that higher price tag. The ApexUp weighted vest is a popular option thanks to its low price point, but it offers more than just savings.

Sources indicate that this vest is built from neoprene (which is the durable synthetic rubber you’ll find in wetsuits) and filled with iron sand, a material that’s denser than natural sand and absorbs less moisture. As a result, it won’t stick to you or clump up when you sweat.

In a recent development, it has a smooth, comfortable feel, with seams that are stitched over with fabric to prevent rubbing and chafing. Wide armholes and an adjustable strap across the chest mean you can get a comfortable fit, no matter your chest size.

In a recent development, the solo strap in ApexUp’s 10-pound version means it’s more likely to shift around during dynamic movements like burpees, making this vest a better choice for things like walking. A lot of the weight in the vest is in the front straps, so just be aware of your posture while you use this. But the mesh storage pocket in back is secure and roomy enough for your phone, which is a nice feature if you want to free up your hands.

It has been revealed that A common complaint with this vest is the smell, which may be due to that neoprene cover. If you notice it and it bothers you, just let the vest air out a little before using it. Also, be aware that the ApexUp vest doesn’t allow you to tack on extra weight. But at this low price, you can simply buy a upcoming one when you’re ready for more resistance and still come out on top, price-wise.

The best weighted vest is one you’ll actually wear, and the Stakt Adjustable Weighted Vest makes that part easy. Instead of looking like tactical gear, its streamlined neoprene construction fits close to the body and feels more like a weighted garment.

In a recent development, one way WH fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT likes to use weighted vests in her own training and with her training clients is to increase proprioception, or awareness of the body’s position in space. Because the Stakt vest distributes weight around the torso instead of loading only the shoulders, it can provide helpful feedback for connecting with the core and postural muscles during movement.

It has been revealed that the Stakt weighted vest starts at six pounds and a two-pound zip-on extension brings it up to eight pounds. Grief tested both configurations while walking, doing chores around her apartment, doing pushups, and adding it to a functional training workout. It delivered comfortable, evenly distributed weight that fits and feels more like an additional clothing layer than a traditional weighted vest.

The aluminum front buckles feel sturdy. The shoulder straps use a hook-and-loop adjustment system, so once Grief found the right adjustment, it was a set-it-and-forget-it situation, and the straps stayed put. “I didn’t have to interrupt any workout to readjust them,” she mentioned.

A porous mesh liner creates a comfortable buffer between the body and the neoprene, which adds some breathability. It also zips out for washing, which is a helpful feature, especially considering that this vest is worn close to the body. The vest also has a mesh pocket for small essentials. Its reflective detailing is minimal though, so you’ll want additional visibility gear when walking in low-light conditions.

Read More: Stakt Weighted Vest Review.

It has been revealed that if you’re looking for an adjustable-weight option ideal for specific functional training exercises and rucking, the Hyper Vest Elite from Hyperwear is highly customizable. I tested the 10-pound model, which is weighted with 66 individual 2.25-ounce stainless steel bars, each with its own little pocket.

In a recent development, if you prefer heavier weights, 15- and 20-pound options are available. Plus, you can purchase a box of individual weights to load up your vest (each pocket can fit two 2.25-ounce weights).

I wore it during multiple 60-minute walks, squats, pull-ups, push-ups, and back extensions. With the full 10 pounds loaded on my body, I found it really difficult to do pull-ups and push-ups. However, when I removed some of the weights from the individual pockets, it made for a more manageable load.

According to recent reports, that said, I’m not sure how realistic it is to load up these tiny weights into individual pouches when switching between exercises. I think it’s a great feature, but personally, I’d design my workouts to ensure I didn’t have to adjust the weights more than once.

There are adjustable cords on each side to cinch or loosen for your preferred fit, but you won’t find shoulder strap adjustments like on the Omorpho vests. I also noticed the Hyperwear vest sits nearly five inches lower on my torso than the Omorpho vest. It doesn’t dig into my hips, but I notice it grazes my lower back when walking. It’s not a deal breaker, but I prefer shorter styles. Four size options are available: small, medium, large, and extra large.

Sources indicate that as for material, I appreciate the heavy-duty construction of this vest, which is made with Cordura, a synthetic, tear-resistant fabric popular for backpacks and military clothing. It will hold up for years, even if you blueprint to go hiking or wear it in the elements. I also like the reflective strips at the zipper and across the chest for increased visibility outdoors.

If you’re looking for a weighted vest with resistance that pushes your limits while not disrupting your range of motion, this one by Vivitory checks the box. Despite the non-cropped fit, it still stays in place with only two adjustable straps and distributes weight evenly (11 pounds for the medium size and 18 pounds for the large size).

WH art director Christine Giordano was pleasantly surprised by how light it felt compared to holding it. “I was nervous it was going to be too heavy for me or cause pain in my lower back, but I was wrong,” states Giordano. “It didn’t bounce up and down or move all over—it stayed snug to my body while not being too hot and bulky.”.

According to recent reports, she loves wearing it during easy walks when waiting around for her kids’ sporting events or for more intense workouts, such as CrossFit or burpees. “I’m not a huge fan of dumbbell step-ups, so I tried it with the vest for the added weight without leaning forward,” she says.

As for the material, it’s made with neoprene, a synthetic rubber resistant to sweat that Giordano notes she found to be breathable. There are also reflective strips on the vest for visibility during dawn or dusk, and a small pouch at the back for holding essentials.

Industry observers note that if you get seriously sweaty during cardio or weightlifting, this 12-pound Reebok weighted vest is an option in hot summer temps. The back has a breathable ventilation panel that allows air to circulate.

WH contributor Korin Miller has recently added it to her workout gear lineup. “I like to go hard with my workouts, and I get really sweaty as a result—I appreciate the open-air design of this vest so I can cool off,” states Miller. “That, combined with the airy fabric, means I won’t end up with the vest sticking against my skin during workouts.”.

According to recent reports, aside from its sweat-wicking properties, its two adjustable straps allow for a customized fit during a variety of workouts. For Miller, specifically walking, cycling, rowing, and bodyweight movements, such as planks and squats.

In a recent development, but, it’s crucial to note this model isn’t ideal for jumping. “Those extra weights can flap around during bigger movements like running and HIIT workouts—basically anything that has you jumping up and down,” says Miller.

Read More: Reebok Weighted Vest Review.

According to recent reports, the Omorpho G-Vest Icon is a quality choice for runners and HIIT workouts, given its snug fit and moderate weight that doesn’t feel like too much. The design is really similar to Omorpho’s OG model, with soft neoprene-style fabric, stainless steel ball bearings embedded into the fabric, and waist and shoulder adjustments for a custom fit.

Sources indicate that the main difference is the adjustable weight and reflective strips throughout for extra visibility during night runs. The adjustable weight system is genius. It involves “G-Packs” of varying weights that snap in and out, allowing you to tack on additional, evenly distributed weight fast. (Just a heads up: A set of three G-Packs that brings the weight up to 12 pounds costs an extra $129.).

Sources indicate that we also like that the encased stainless steel weights are not featured through the chest area. If you want to wear the G-Vest Icon with just a sports bra, you won’t have any irritation from high-impact movements.

For reference, the weights go up the entirety of the front panels on the men’s version. While the vest’s fitted style is ideal for runs, its six-pound weight means it’s better suited for things like short runs and sprints.

One downside is that the neoprene-style fabric made our tester sweat a ton when worn with layers. “My first experience with the vest was under my winter jacket on a 10-degree day during an hour-long walk,” WH contributor Korin Miller says. “I sweat my butt off despite the cold temperatures, compared to having sweat evaporate from my skin at the gym.”.

Read More: Omorpho G-Vest Icon Review.

It has been revealed that besides being a WH Fitness Awards 2025 winner, the Empower Weighted Vest is the only vest we’ve seen with a cross-style fit. It’s designed specifically to fit women’s curves while offering supreme support for the shoulder blades. The fit is compact with less material at the sides, while the straps are fully adjustable.

While its main highlight is being a custom fit for women, another unique feature is six removable one-pound bags (three in the front and three in the back pockets). In the 10-pound model (weight ranges from eight to 16 pounds), the vest can go as low as four pounds when the weights are removed if you’re seeking only light resistance.

Industry observers note that WH health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, uses it for taking her workouts to the next level. “It elevates my walks, helps my core activate more, and makes my bodyweight exercises harder,” she indicates. Her only complaint is that the removable weights can make it feel bulky and interfere with hitting the full range of motion with a handful of exercises. “If I wanted to do crunches, I couldn’t lie on my back without it arching, and I couldn’t do supermans from my stomach because the bags in the front made it so I couldn’t lie flat,” she says. “During other strength exercises like squats, it hit the top of my thigh and prevented me from moving down further.” Perhaps it’s best to use the added pocket weights only during walks.

As for material, it’s neoprene for optimal sweat resistance, like the Vivitory and Prodigen weighted vests.

Not everyone wants or needs the 20-pound resistance TRX’s Hexgrip Weighted Vest can offer. But this vest is adjustable, allowing you to tweak the weight in one-pound increments, giving you room to grow up to that 20 pounds. So, if you want to use it as a 10-pound vest to start, more power to you.

This sturdy vest helps you get a secure fit with the help of three wide Velcro straps, making it a solid option for dynamic movements, some cardio workouts, and general strength training. The neoprene inner is comfortable against your skin, while the snug fit and smartly positioned weights mean you don’t have to stress about the vest moving around on you while you work out.

While it’s on the heavier end, it’s not bulky. As a result, you can still feel comfortable doing your usual range of motion. Just a heads up: Some of the weights are positioned across the chest, which may feel more noticeable if you have larger breasts. But those adjustable straps mean you can lower or raise the shoulder straps to find a position that’s more comfortable for you.

The weights slip into individual pockets to prevent them from shifting around, but make sure they’re secured well before you start your workout. (Some people have reported them sliding out.) Because the adjustment process takes some time, this isn’t a vest you’ll want to adjust mid-workout. This vest also comes in a 40-pound version, although most exercisers will do best with the 20-pounder as a heavy option.

Industry observers note that if you have broader shoulders, the RITFIT has fully adjustable straps. They're spaced further apart—one sits higher on your chest and the other closer to your waist.

It can be more comfortable if you have a larger chest, while it may run bigger on smaller frames. It also has mesh pockets to store your keys and phone.

The load on a weighted vest can range from 3 to over 30 pounds, depending on the style and brand. If you’ve never used a weighted vest or are upcoming to resistance training, I recommend starting with a lighter option between 3 and 10 pounds. Our best overall pick is optimal for newbies since it’s five pounds.

In a recent development, heavier vests are ideal for loading bodyweight exercises like push-ups, pull-ups, squats, and walking lunges. They can also be used for walking, hiking, or rucking, depending on your fitness level. Lighter vests are ideal for speed training like sprinting, interval training, and plyometric exercises like box jumps, burpees, or jump roping.

Recent findings suggest that durable materials such as Cordura, nylon, and polyester are less likely to tear from constant wear during intense movement. All of the picks on this list are made from either of these three fabrics, and I found they perform well during explosive workouts and cardio. They also wick away sweat, which is a must for ultimate comfort. As for fit, I love an adjustable closure system with a zipper or buckles at the front, waist, and shoulders for customizing the fit.

Sources indicate that since 2020, we’ve updated this story and tested every major weighted vest on the market. I’m a certified personal trainer with the National Strength and Conditioning Association. I’ve worked in the health and fitness industry for nine years and have six years of hands-on experience working with clients one-on-one and in small group settings. With experience testing and reviewing hundreds of fitness products over the years, I wore select weighted vests for multiple hour-long walks and workouts, including exercises like push-ups, pull-ups, lunges, planks, and box jumps. I paid close attention to the material to see how it held up against sweat, fit for comfort, and weight for resistance levels. I also kept notes of my likes and dislikes.

WH editors, including associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, art director Christine Giordano, and contributor Korin Miller, also tested a few options and provided extensive notes on their experiences with them. Read on for our thoughts on the best weighted vests for women, as well as some other recommendations we like but haven't tested personally.

Ah, the rancher jacket. It’s a double-sided gem, one that both looks the part but delivers even in the most rugged conditions. This fine option from Flint and Tinder is flannel-lined to fend off the chilly bite, as well as quilted and stuffed with insulation for good measure. That means even the nastiest of winds won’t bother him while he’s out chopping wood for the campfire. In a recent development, take all the bear-, weather-, and bomb-proofness of Yeti’s Loadout GoBox (and coolers) and shrink it down to a 1-liter case that’s perfect for phones, wallets, watches, AirPods, protein bars, or anything for your EDC. I've used it so far on camping trips to go screen-free, as well as a few canoe rides where I still wanted to have my phone around (but avoid it getting wet).

A substantial part of nailing the marks in the outdoor apparel realm is conquering both flexibility and insulation. You know, like this stretchy number from Mountain Hardwear. It’s plenty warm, packs down like a charm, and moves with your natural motions, never pulling or tugging. It helps that it looks sharp and touts elastic cuff bindings to lock in the warmth on those chilly evenings and mornings. This one is a great gift for all types of outdoorsmen, from campers and hikers to anglers and skiers. We found that the climbers here at MH especially liked this one, drawn to the agile design.

This will come in handy for spontaneous adventurers. It’s a handy, pocket-sized kit that has 48 tools useful in almost any outdoor survival situation. Plus, it looks like a freakin' grenade. How gift-worthy is that?

Camp Snap brings a bit of that retro joy to your outdoor adventures. A screen-free device, it makes you wait (in gleeful anticipation) to see the results of your photographic eye. No, you’re not saying he’s old with this gift. Rather, you’re rewarding his intrepid spirit and encouraging him to venture even deeper into those topsy-turvy trails. Portable, lightweight, and strong, you can pull these puppies out of your pack and deploy them in an instant with a single button press.

The best of the outdoors is usually an off-the-grid sort of thing but a little tech can help you enjoy remote areas even more. Take the latest from Garmin, part of an esteemed line of communication devices that can go deep, deep into the brush. Here’s a pair for the trail-running novice and seasoned vet alike. Under the hood, an improved midsole that rebounds like an NBA-level power forward and dual mid-foot webbing reinforcements to assist those active feet. And the details add up, from the padded collar to the stay-in-place tongue wings, making for a smooth trek even way, way down (or up) the trail.

Industry observers note that what takes a hoodie into the high-performance echelon and helps it excel there? Oh, and the raglan sleeves and elastic ends keep things comfortable and secure the warmth. It’s an added bonus that the fit is just about perfect, the hood wears brilliantly, and the whole thing can fend off even the thickest brush and snags. As Marmot rightfully claims, this one breathes like a feather and feels like a fleece. Usually it’s one or the other but not here. Gift this one to that restless outdoorsy soul who stays active year-round.

Taking the enhanced vision category into the unexpected realm of cool, Nocs is up to good work. Waterproof, they can accompany any trek, on land or water, in summer or winter, and that goes for all types of outdoors enthusiasts, from casual birders and hikers to backcountry pros and road trippers who like to hit the pullouts and take it all in. Compact with full-size clarity, these binocs do what many twice their size try to do, so store ’em in a small pack or wear ‘em over your neck with ease.

According to recent reports, flannels are a staple in an outdoorsman's wardrobe. If he has yet to try Outerknown's Blanket Shirt, now is the time to gift him one. You really can’t miss with a trusty multitool. And there’s no more trusty versions out there than the Skeletool CX from Leatherman. Tech Report: Europe’s electric car sales jump 49% as global EV sales grow

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1056 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026.
  • It has been revealed that drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to new data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
  • Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026. But that North American rebound comes with a big catch.

It has been revealed that drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to new data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That’s down 3% from September, but it brings sales for the first 10 months of 2026 to 17.5 million – up 5% from the same period last year.

Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.

Europe sold 510,000 EVs in October, up 36% year over year. Fully electric cars did most of the work: BEV sales rose 49%, while plug-in hybrids grew 7%.

That puts October’s growth ahead of Europe’s 31% increase for the year so far. The region has now sold 4.5 million EVs in 2026.

Sources indicate that sales fell 17% from September’s record, but September got a boost from the UK’s twice-yearly registration plate change. The year-over-year figures give a clearer view of how promptly the market is growing.

Sources indicate that germany’s EV share topped 45% of upcoming car sales, its highest level since December 2022. That earlier peak came as buyers rushed to get cars before subsidy cuts took effect. Fully electric car sales in Germany rose almost 80% from a year earlier to more than 95,000.

In a recent development, UK EV sales increased 30%. That’s particularly notable because the Electric Car Grant was already available in October 2025, although fewer models qualified then. So this growth comes against a market that was already getting government support.

And in Portugal, EVs accounted for 55% of newly introduced car sales in October, following a sharp rise in their market share over the past few months.

Sources indicate that north American EV sales rose 24% year over year to 130,000 in October, the region’s first annual increase of 2026. Sales were flat from September, while the year-to-date decline narrowed to 21%, from 24% a month earlier. The region has sold 1.3 million EVs so far this year.

US EV sales reached around 110,000 units in October.

But here’s the catch: October 2025 was the first month after the federal EV tax credit expired. The credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and sales dropped sharply afterward.

According to recent reports, october 2026 is therefore being compared with a month when sales plummeted. A positive annual number doesn’t mean US demand has returned to its pre-expiration level.

“October is the first month compared against a period without the US federal tax credit, and the US market has stabilized at a lower level rather than recovered,” mentioned Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.

The flat month-over-month figure helps tell that story: Sales have steadied, but the market is operating from a lower base.

China sold 1.14 million EVs in October, up 5% from September but down 12% year over year. That annual decline was smaller than September’s 18% drop.

Sales through October reached 9.1 million, down 11%, compared with a 13% year-to-date decline at the end of September.

Even with fewer EVs being sold, their share of China’s new car market reached a fresh high. That’s because the wider passenger car market is shrinking faster.

Chinese automakers are continuing to produce vehicles and look overseas for buyers. Passenger car exports of fresh energy vehicles – China’s category covering BEVs and PHEVs – reached nearly 600,000 in October. That’s another monthly record, up from 558,000 in September.

Sources indicate that those exports face more pressure ahead. The EU has agreed to cap imports of Chinese-built hybrids, and China will reduce its EV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027.

Outside China, Europe, and North America, EV sales rose 85% year over year to 300,000 in October. Those markets have bought 2.6 million EVs so far in 2026, up 93%.

Australia’s sales jumped more than 200% in October, and EVs have gained market share sharply this year. But that hasn’t translated into healthy dealer profits, according to Benchmark. More brands, many of them Chinese, are competing for buyers, spreading sales across more companies and squeezing dealer margins.

Brazil’s growth has also been huge, although Benchmark cautions that some of its drivers are temporary. Importers brought vehicles in ahead of phased tariff increases, a fuel crisis pushed more buyers toward EVs, and BYD increased production at its Brazilian factory.

Recent findings suggest that nothing like consumer economics to drive sales. Local story about consumer economics: Windturbines on land is not popular. However, the locals realised they could heat their home for $300/year (in Denmark(!)) with these wind turbines and then they were tolerated! Same with cars - people gravitate to cheaper alternatives despite the more frequent charging and initial higher prices.

As the tariff increases take full effect and fuel price pressure eases, Benchmark expects those boosts to fade. BYD’s local production, which will also supply Argentina and Mexico, is set to become the main remaining support for that growth.

Honda’s $2,000 electric moped is a winner. So why can’t Americans buy it?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting fresh models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine.
  • Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.
  • It has been revealed that we first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the tech giant revealed plans to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting fresh models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine. It’s a modest little electric scooter called the Honda UC3, and with prices now dipping close to $2,000 in local markets, it’s the kind of affordable electric two-wheeler that many Americans would probably love to get their hands on.

Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.

It has been revealed that we first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the tech giant revealed plans to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam. Designed as an electric equivalent to a 110cc gasoline-powered scooter, the UC3 is built for practical everyday transportation rather than weekend joyrides.

But don’t let its modest appearance fool you. The UC3 packs a 6 kW (8 hp) electric motor capable of reaching approximately 50 mph (80 km/h), making it more than capable of handling typical urban commuting.

In a recent development, its 3.2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery provides up to 76 miles (122 km) of range under WMTC testing. Unlike Honda’s other electric scooters that use removable batteries, the UC3 has a permanently installed battery that charges directly on the bike.

There’s also a full-color TFT display, smartphone connectivity, three riding modes, reverse gear, and a generous 26-liter under-seat storage compartment.

And perhaps most importantly, it comes from Honda, a tech giant with decades of experience building reliable, affordable motorcycles.

The UC3 originally introduced in Vietnam with prices starting around 78.5 million Vietnamese dong, or roughly $3,000. However, recent reports from Vietnamese dealerships show incentives bringing prices down to around 54 million dong, equivalent to approximately $2,100.

That’s a pretty compelling price for a 50 mph (80 km/h) electric scooter from one of the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturers.

But despite its appeal, Honda hasn’t confirmed any looks to bring the UC3 to the United States.

And frankly, I wouldn’t hold my breath.

In much of Southeast Asia, scooters are everyday transportation, with millions of riders using them for commuting, shopping, and practically everything else. In the US, motorcycles are much more commonly recreational vehicles, and the market for small, practical scooters is comparatively tiny.

I'm hoping scooters like this take over the world, the sooner the better. Anyone who's travelled in any cities in Asian, India, or most of Europe, there's always a constant background whine of 2-stroke scooters, day and night.

According to recent reports, I would have thought these kinds of markets would have already transitioned to EV - in addition to the annoying sound, those 2-stroke engines spew out an order of magnitude more pollution than most ICE vehicles. I guess it's been a cost concern - this scooter should be cheap enough to take over the world.

Add in the costs of US regulatory certification, establishing parts and service support, and navigating a market where many buyers expect motorcycles to handle highway speeds, and the business case becomes considerably less attractive.

That’s unfortunate, because the UC3 looks like exactly the kind of electric two-wheeler that could make a real difference in American cities.

It’s affordable, practical, fast enough for most city streets, and backed by a manufacturer that isn’t going anywhere.

Now if only Honda would give Americans a chance to buy one.

Puma Speedcat OG Review: A Style Writer’s Honest Opinion After 2 Months of Testing
