📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins.
  • It has been revealed that lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena.
  • District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins. Before bringing a new installment of her bestselling dystopian saga to the big screen, the two join forces to envision how the fictional world of Panem will take shape. “I go to New York each time, and we sit in a conference room at Scholastic,” indicates Lawrence, who has directed five of the franchise’s six films. “We go through the book page by page and beat out what we think the movie is going to look like.”.

It has been revealed that lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena. Set twenty-four years before the original The Hunger Games (2012) plotline, the prequel follows District 12’s sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada)—the future mentor (played by Woody Harrelson) to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson)—as he is selected to fight in the Second Quarter Quell, a particularly sadistic rendition of the Games held every twenty-five years.

District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.

Though the dystopia is set in a future North America, the previous prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023), drew from the architecture of 1940s and ’50s postwar Berlin to depict evil President Snow’s rise to tyranny. Set forty years later, Sunrise explores Panem at a fresh stage of its evolution. Designed by returning production designer Uli Hanisch, the film follows Haymitch from his impoverished mining district, which barely evolves throughout the series’s sixty-five year timeline, to the opulent Capitol, whose extravagance is expressed through a 1970s-inflected visual lexicon.

In a recent development, “I realized the ’70s fall right smack in the middle between that movie and the originals, so we could lean into that,” says Lawrence. Hanisch and his team incorporated references to Andy Warhol, Studio 54, and the decade’s psychedelic color palette, appropriating its progressive spirit to convey the Capitol’s opulence and authoritarianism—and, particularly in the arena, using the aesthetic as a means of deception. “To turn the ’70s style from something progressive, liberal, young, and open-minded into something evil is a twist,” says Hanisch. “But that is the key to the entire film’s design.”.

Haymitch and Maysilee as allies in the arena. The forest portion was filmed separately near Cologne, Germany.

Industry observers note that the stylistic choice is also a poignant nod to Collins’s original inspiration for the book series. The 1970s marked a transformation in American television: as color TVs became ubiquitous in households across the country, sporting spectacles, variety shows, and beauty pageants flourished, establishing cultural touchstones that would help shape the contemporary reality programming Collins critiques and satirizes in The Hunger Games. “I was flipping through the channels one night between reality television programs and actual footage of the Iraq War, when the idea came to me,” Collins recalled in a 2018 interview with The New York Times. The juxtaposition inspired her to explore just-war theory for young people through an authoritarian dystopia in which mass entertainment is an instrument of political control.

From an abandoned rural steel mill to authoritarian monuments from postwar Berlin, the film draws on politically charged German sites to capture Panem at a pivotal stage in its political and architectural evolution.

Recent findings suggest that production Designer Uli Hanisch at the District 12 set. “District 12 is the most sentimental set to me because I’d known this site near my hometown my entire life,” Hanisch says.

In a recent development, to recreate the Appalachian-inspired, deteriorating industrial landscape of District 12 that was shot in Atlanta in the original series, the production utilized a sprawling abandoned steel mill in Duisburg, Germany, Hanisch’s hometown. “I wish we had it in the original movies, because it is an unbelievable space,” Lawrence claims of the post-industrial, rural landscape, which also appeared in The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, Hanisch’s first film in the franchise. “Everywhere you look is exactly how I have always imagined District 12.”.

Sources indicate that while District 12 was filmed near Atlanta in the original films, director Francis Lawrence’s fascination with German architecture brought production to Berlin for The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. It was there that he began collaborating with Berlin-based production designer Hanisch, who proposed this steel mill nearby his hometown for the upcoming location. Upon seeing photographs, Lawrence exclaimed, “Are you kidding me? ... Let’s go tomorrow,” and promptly flew out to see it for himself.

The production designer added modest huts at the edge of a nearby quarry to recreate the Seam, home to Haymitch, his girlfriend Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak), and fellow tribute Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), its humble dwellings contrasting the more prosperous merchant district inhabited by fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace).

“Unlike the Capitol, District 12 doesn't evolve stylistically throughout the films. Nobody is investing in it, and everything is gradually deteriorating,” Hanisch explains. The vivid purples and oranges of the Capitol’s ‘70s palette are notably absent, only appearing prominently in propaganda decorating the reaping square, including Hunger Games campaign materials and posters portraying Snow as Panem’s number-one Peacekeeper.

Druscilla in the Capitol before the tribute interviews, which is broadcast to all of Panem.

According to recent reports, in the Capitol, however, the architecture takes on a distinctly ‘70s flair. Rooted in the Roman concept of panem et circenses, or “bread and circuses,” from which Panem takes its name, the architecture reinforces the government’s manipulation through spectacle. In the background is Berlin's International Congress Centrum, a colossal, aluminum-clad convention center that opened in 1979, which Lawrence describes as “Cold War-era Berlin showing off in a modern way.” As West Berlin’s most expensive postwar building, the futuristic complex was publicly subsidised to showcase economic prosperity and technological advancement—an evocative backdrop for the Capitol’s own display of authoritarianism.

“It’s a time of peace for the Capitol with no rebel attacks, so Snow's had time to build the city up in a way that is an extravagant show of power,” Lawrence explains. The chariot parade, which introduces the tributes before the Games, similarly unfolds against the historically-charged Berlin Olympiastadion, which was designed by Werner March for the 1936 Olympics under Nazi Germany to project state power and an illusion of timeless permanence.

The upstairs library in Plutarch’s home, which he inherited from the Heavensbee dynasty. Reflecting the Capitol’s classic style, it contrasts the Plutarch’s modern downstairs salon which features Warhol-inspired portraits, including one of director Lawrence.

The Capitol's grandeur is also exhibited inside the mansion of Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), a cameraman with historic ties to Panem’s ruling class. “This was one of my favorite sets because of the scope and scale” Lawrence says, noting how its excess reflects the dynasty's immense wealth. Filmed at Berlin's late-1960s modernist Congress Center, the circular residence required twenty-five vans of retro-modern furniture to fill it. The salon, decked in vibrant 1970s furnishings and Warhol-inspired art, showcases Plutarch's modern sensibilities, in stark contrast to the upstairs library inherited from his family. “We wanted to distinguish Plutarch from the dynasty he comes from,” Lawrence explains, reflecting on how the expansive volumes must be a facade of intellectual sophistication.

It has been revealed that the set decoration department spent weeks hand-folding and assembling thousands of hollow cardboard books, interspersed with real volumes, including a collection of Edgar Allan Poe’s poetry, which Plutarch references to Haymitch. “We imagined Plutarch might actually be the first Heavensbee to read some of those books,” Hanisch notes. “He even says the library is one of the few worthwhile things his ancestors accomplished.”.

It has been revealed that the library's custom-built curved bookshelves envelope the characters, symbolising the insularity of Capitol society. “Circles represent both inclusion and exclusion,” Hanisch says. “If you are in the circle, you're in. And if you're not, you're out.” As fans of the franchise will know, Plutarch (originally played by Philip Seymour Hoffman) later reveals himself as a double agent and leader of the underground rebellion against Snow’s regime.

The aspect ratio expands as Haymitch ascends into the eye-shaped arena, emphasizing the landscape’s immersive scale and beauty. While scouting locations, Lawrence drew inspiration from the dramatic landscapes in Terrence Malick’s A Hidden Life. “I had that in my head, only it was a little trippier. The Asturias were perfect,” he recalls. The kaleidoscopic design also inspired the official logo of the 50th Hunger Games, extending the arena’s psychedelic imagery into the Capitol’s propaganda.

The Quarter Quell arena, in particular, embodies the surreal, fantastical ethos of the 1970s that permeates the film, illustrating how the Capitol exploits beauty to disguise its underlying manipulation and brutality. “As I was reading with Suzanne, I stated there was an Alice in Wonderland-like element to it, which made me think of the song ‘White Rabbit,’ which made me think of the late ’60s, early ’70s,” Lawrence recalls. “That kind of broke something open for me.”.

It has been revealed that designed in the shape of an eye, the eight to ten mile arena serves as a metaphor for the Capitol's omnipresent surveillance. A golden Cornucopia forms its pupil; vibrant meadows its iris; and the surrounding mountain ranges its whites. In the book, Haymitch describes the especially lethal arena masquerading as an idyllic landscape as a “poisonous beauty of an arena.”.

It has been revealed that lawrence and Haymitch in the arena. The physical flowers were concentrated in the foreground, while visual effects extended the colorful landscape into the distance.

Seeking to capture as much natural landscape as possible, Hanisch and location manager Klaus große Darrelmann discovered a remote valley in Asturias, Spain, surrounded by the Cantabrian Mountains. Transforming the isolated valley into a psychedelic paradise proved an enormous undertaking.“The arena was our nemesis,” claims Hanisch, recalling how the production had to bring extensive resources to the remote terrain. “You can't even imagine how far away it was or how hard it was to get to.” Crews spent weeks individually installing hundreds of thousands of artificial flowers throughout the meadows and forests.

Sources indicate that despite the arena’s dreamlike beauty, water sources, flowers, and vegetation conceal deadly poisons. “It’s the most colorful and playful dystopia you’ll ever see,” producer Nina Jacobson states. Perhaps more than anywhere else in Panem, the arena encapsulates how the Capitol weaponizes the electric zeitgeist of the ‘70s as an instrument of control. “To have something so overwhelmingly beautiful and seductive but poisonous and deadly is very cruel,” Hanisch says. “That contradiction captures the mentality of Panem at this point in its history.”.

I Tried Adding 10 Minutes of Daily Mobility to My Routine for Two Weeks. Here’s How My Body—And Mind—Changed

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort.
  • Mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk.
  • It has been revealed that this style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort. The natural loss of lean muscle mass and skin elasticity that occurs at this stage of life makes me more mindful of my body and overall well-being. So, I’ve declared this my year of wellness. As part of it, I have been working on adding small bouts of movement that manageably fit into my daily life. Mobility work felt like one of the best ways to do that.

Mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk. Mobility training focuses on controlled, active movement through a joint’s full range of motion, says Matthew Cifelli, PT, DPT, CSCS, of Attain Physical Therapy.

It has been revealed that this style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving. But as you age or spend extended periods of time being sedentary, it’s common for muscles to tighten, joints to stiffen, and movement to become less efficient.

In a recent development, “Limited mobility forces the body to compensate with inefficient patterns, increasing the risk of pain, balance challenges, and injury,” says Cifelli. Maintaining mobility, on the other hand, “supports independence, joint health, and the ability to move confidently through life.”.

That’s why I recently decided to add just 10 minutes of mobility work to my daily routine for two weeks. Here’s exactly what I did—and how my body changed.

Mobility is “not just about ‘feeling loose,’” says Cifelli. “It's about teaching the body to use its flexibility in real movement.” It’s a mix of static stretching and flexibility work that focuses on muscle length. “Mobility training targets how well a joint moves and how well you control that motion, which requires coordinated muscle activation and joint stability.”.

It has been revealed that and just a few minutes a day of mobility work can help boost circulation, lubricate the joints, alleviate muscle tension, and improve confidence in daily movement. “Even short sessions, when done daily, create meaningful cumulative change,” he says.

In a recent development, my routine included a combination of exercises and hold times I learned from Portia Page, CPT, in addition to a couple of stretches my physical therapist recommended incorporating into my home regimen. I performed each exercise for one minute, one time through.

Recent findings suggest that during the first week of my experiment, I eased into my 10-minute mobility routine. I was eager to see how it could help improve my “desk body,” a.k.a. tight hips, tense hamstrings, and lower back and neck tension.

I did the workout every morning around 8 a.m. before diving into the madness of the day. It was pretty seamless to add to my mornings, since I have a dedicated workout space in my home, though the routine doesn’t require much space or equipment. Plus, I’m someone who craves routine. Sticking to the same time each morning made this fitness habit sustainable.

Sources indicate that from the get-go, it was clear my body was tense and in desperate need of some stretching and mobility work. My legs, back, and hips all felt stiff at the beginning of the workout. Certain exercises, like the standing forward fold, hip flexor stretch, and supine figure-four stretch were more challenging than the rest. For example, during the first week, I found it difficult to touch the floor when doing the forward fold, so I didn’t force it.

By the end of each session, my body was definitely a bit more relaxed, but I knew I needed to stick with mobility work for more than just a week or two in order to achieve meaningful, lasting results.

It has been revealed that I was a dancer growing up, and my body was much more flexible then than it is now. While the Pilates classes I attend three to four times a week have definitely helped me stretch and strengthen my body, a dedicated mobility routine felt like exactly what the doctor ordered. I didn’t realize it would help me in my classes, too. By the end of week one, I felt I was able to move through a more seamless range of motion in certain Pilates exercises like the mermaid and the straight-back hinge on the short box.

It has been revealed that heading into week two, I found myself looking forward to my morning mobility session. It started to feel like more of a natural segue into my day, similar to brushing my teeth, taking my vitamins, or getting dressed. Once I wrapped up stretching and sat down at my desk, my body felt more limber and relaxed as I started work. However, after a couple hours of sitting, I felt much more tense again. The experiment taught me to be mindful of that: My body needs movement throughout the day—not just first thing in the morning.

I felt inspired by this healthy mobility habit and how great I feel afterward, so I wanted to keep the momentum going. During week two, I started building other healthy habits, like getting up to walk around my kitchen and living room every hour and going on a longer brisk walk at the end of the day. Both helped me stay limber throughout the day, rather than just in the morning. My hope is that, with all of these bouts of movement combined, sitting won’t undo all of the wonderful benefits I get from my stretching routine.

Sources indicate that by the end of the second week, I was pleased that my body felt more accustomed to the dedicated mobility work than it had during week one. The more challenging stretches also became slightly easier, which made me feel like I was making genuine progress.

The routine became a no-brainer—a staple, if you will—in my morning routine: I’d wake up, brew a soothing latte, and get to work on my yoga mat. It also sparked the desire to get up and move more during the workday rather than remain hunched over my laptop for an extended period of time.

Because I experienced the tension-relieving benefits of this mobility work almost immediately after each session during week two, I’m now inspired to do it at both the start and end of my day. It’s a great way to ease any built-up stiffness after a long day at my desk before slipping into bed.

That said, one thing I’d love to continue working on is my posture. I didn’t experience any groundbreaking improvements during this two-week timeframe, but I’m hopeful that I’ll make progress down the line. I’m also curious to see whether being consistent with this mobility routine long-term will help my body—especially my hips and lower back—feel less stiff after sitting or lounging for longer periods.

Sources indicate that consistency is key. As with any workout, consistency is essential for success. But alas, it’s something I’ve struggled with over the years. Hectic work weeks filled with deadlines and appointments typically push my fitness to the back burner.

Sources indicate that however, during this two-week test period, I was incredibly determined to carve out 10 minutes each day for my stretching regimen, and I’m so glad I did. Sticking with this fitness habit helped me feel better mentally and physically. My body started to feel more flexible and limber by the end of the two-week period—something I don’t think I would have experienced if I were inconsistent with my efforts.

Try this 15-minute mobility routine.

According to Page, a mere 5 to 10 minutes a day of mobility work can make a noticeable difference over time if you’re consistent with the habit. She recommends thinking of stretching “not as a luxury but as basic maintenance for your body—like brushing your teeth.”.

Industry observers note that kickstarting the day with fitness can promote other healthy habits. Starting the day with mobility work inspired me to follow other healthy habits throughout. After all, I was already off to a solid start and wanted to keep that momentum going strong.

Recent findings suggest that following each mobility session, I felt accomplished, energized, and ready to tackle the day. I found myself sticking with my regular Pilates workouts, making all-around healthier meal choices, snacking less, and adding brief “movement snacks” to my afternoons to break up the time spent sitting at my desk.

According to recent reports, mobility is a low-barrier starting point for movement. What I love best about this mobility workout? I don’t need to leave the comfort of my home or have access to fancy equipment. I’ve seamlessly incorporated these exercises into my self-care routine, and it just takes 10 minutes of my morning before I dive into work deadlines and commitments.

While there’s always room for improvement—and I’d like to add even more stretches to my routine—I felt incredibly accomplished overall with only a 10-minute routine. I’m hopeful that, by starting now and being consistent with mobility training, I can help prepare my body to tackle everyday tasks with ease. This training can also help me stay mobile, confident, and independent in my adventurous lifestyle for the long term.

Mercedes-Benz Will Sell a C111 Rotary Supercar Prototype for the First Time in History

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there’s no shortage of rare, collectable, crazy-desirable classic Mercedes-Benz vehicles out there for the discerning car collector.
  • But no matter how rich, how connected, how much of a master of the universe you are, you’ve never been able to buy one of Mercedes-Benz’s most ground-breaking machines: the rotary-powered C111.
  • Fans of the brand certainly need no introduction to this wedge-shaped beauty, but for those of you who might not be as current on your Mercedes history, the C111 was revealed at the 1969 International Motor Show (IAA) in Frankfurt, less than two months after Neil Armstrong plopped his boots on the moon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there’s no shortage of rare, collectable, crazy-desirable classic Mercedes-Benz vehicles out there for the discerning car collector. Some of the Three-Pointed Star’s cars have gone down in history among the most expensive automobiles ever sold; there’s the $11.8 million 1936 Mercedes-Benz 540 K Special Roadster by Sindelfingen, the $10.2 million 2002 Mercedes-Benz CLK GTR Roadster, and of course, the 1955 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupé that sold for over $140 million back in 2022, making it the world’s most valuable car.

But no matter how rich, how connected, how much of a master of the universe you are, you’ve never been able to buy one of Mercedes-Benz’s most ground-breaking machines: the rotary-powered C111. Or at least, that was the case. Come next year, for the very first time, one lucky person will be able to take the Apollo-era wundercar home.

Fans of the brand certainly need no introduction to this wedge-shaped beauty, but for those of you who might not be as current on your Mercedes history, the C111 was revealed at the 1969 International Motor Show (IAA) in Frankfurt, less than two months after Neil Armstrong plopped his boots on the moon. The idea was to create a gullwinged successor to the iconic W198-gen 300SL that dominated racing in the 1950s, packed with then-impressive technology: Wankel rotary engines, fiberglass bodywork, and multi-link rear suspension, all wrapped in a gorgeous period design.

Sources indicate that yet while 17 prototypes were ultimately made, the car never entered production. Rumor has it that interested parties practically channeled Philip J. Fry shouting “Shut up and take my money” by mailing blank checks to the company’s home office, but Mercedes remarked no dice, citing the Wankel motor’s inability to play nicely with the 1973 oil crisis. (That also kept the motor from winding up in the S-Class, as Mercedes-Benz Classic head of collection Dennis Heck said.) Instead, the copies served as company test beds for years, performing tasks like high-speed testing at Nardo with a variety of different powertrains and aerodynamic kits.

In a recent development, the car in question that will be up for grabs is the third one ever made, a C111-II variant known internally as “Car 33” that comes equipped with its original 2.4-liter 4-rotor engine making 345 horsepower and 289 lb-ft connected to a 5-speed manual gearbox. It was used as part of the Mercedes test fleet, trialing features like anti-lock brakes and a component to empty its twin fuel tanks at even rates—a handy feature in a car capable of 186 miles per hour.

The car was restored to working order two years ago at the Mercedes-Benz Classic Center, although the patina of the Weißherbst-colored exterior and gray-and-white houndstooth patterned interior was kept delightfully intact. As of last month’s photo shoot, its odometer highlighted 24,766 kilometers—15,355 miles.

The C111 in question will hit the auction block on February 3, 2027, at the Palais du Louvre as part of RM Sotheby’s Retromobile Paris auctions, with the funds raised by the sale used to help the automaker further develop the Mercedes-Benz museum in Stuttgart, including the creation of a digital twin of the museum that will let people access it virtually.

Recent findings suggest that given its provenance, I would not expect it to go cheap. Neither does the organization. “We do believe it will come to a significant double-digit euro [price at auction],” CEO of Mercedes-Benz Heritage GmbH Marcus Breitschwerdt told Road & Track.

Industry observers note that “It’s gonna be in excess of twenty-five [million] euros,” RM Sotheby’s president Gord Duff added. “There will be strong activity. It’s one of those things you could never get until now.”.

And if you’re thinking, Ehh, they’ve broken the seal on sales, I’ll wait until they auction off another one—well, you’d better be prepared to hold off until 2051 or so, because Mercedes states this sale includes a contractual commitment that it will not sell any more C111s for the next 25 years. Should you be interested in bidding, you can find out more here.

You can often find him test-driving new cars in New York City, cursing the slow-moving traffic surrounding him.

Here are the coolest e-motorcycles and gear we saw at EICMA 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase.
  • Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.
  • LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the manufacturer has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase. That means that all of the newest electric motorcycle announcements happen in one place, and we get a chance to check out the coolest developments and most interesting newly introduced gear.

Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.

LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the manufacturer has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.

According to recent reports, the new S4 Honcho family was a major focus, including the street-oriented Honcho Street, off-road Honcho Trail, and newly unveiled Honcho Skate, a stripped-down addition to the modular platform. The booth also included LiveWire’s larger S2 electric motorcycles, creating a pretty broad spectrum from lightweight urban machines up through full-size highway-capable electric motorcycles.

Recent findings suggest that the other big piece of the booth was DUST Moto, which LiveWire acquired earlier this year. The production-intent DUST Hightail was displayed alongside the newly revealed DUST Spur, giving LiveWire an immediate presence in the increasingly popular lightweight electric dirt bike category.

Add in STACYC’s electric balance bikes for young riders, and the entire booth almost looked like an electric two-wheeler progression chart: start a kid on a STACYC, move up through lightweight DUST and Honcho machines, and eventually graduate to a full-size LiveWire.

In a recent development, GR1T Motorcycles is a relatively young European electric motorcycle startup that caught my eye at EICMA with its G1 platform, a lightweight electric motorcycle designed and engineered in Italy. The basic recipe is pretty compelling: 130 km/h (81 mph) top speed, 11 kW of continuous power and 26.6 kW (36 hp) peak, all while weighing just 130 kg (287 lb).

Perhaps most importantly for urban riders, its roughly 6 kWh battery is actually split into two removable 3 kWh packs, meaning apartment dwellers can pull the batteries out and charge them inside. They’re big, but removing them is doable.

GR1T’s bikes therefore pack in around 50% more battery capacity than most electric motorcycles in this size and weight class, meaning roughly 50% more range, as well.

There are also some interesting and clever design choices, like the underslung rear suspension and the triple-camera system that includes front and rear dashcams plus a cockpit-facing camera for recording the rider.

The clever part of the overall design scheme is that GR1T isn’t developing a separate platform for every motorcycle. The same basic G1 chassis, motor, batteries, belt drive, and electronics underpin four versions: the G1S Street, G1X Scrambler, G1XR Raider, and utility-oriented G1M Mission.

Prices are set to start at €8,495 including VAT, putting these squarely in that emerging category of reasonably affordable, lightweight electric motorcycles that have enough speed for real-world commuting without chasing superbike performance.

Industry observers note that there’s an crucial caveat, though: these aren’t production motorcycles yet. GR1T indicates it is currently fundraising, with factory development and pre-orders set to follow after funding closes and first deliveries now targeted for the first half of 2028.

So the bikes aren’t quite ready for primetime yet, but it’s definitely a company to watch.

Real Motors brought one of the more visually striking electric motorcycles to EICMA with Project: ARES, a futuristic electric café racer that the American startup describes as an “Electric Analog” machine – basically an attempt to preserve the raw, mechanical connection of motorcycling while ditching unnecessary screens and gadgetry.

And there’s plenty of performance underneath the sci-fi bodywork: Real Motors lists a 75 kW (100 hp) motor, a 15 kWh battery, a 120 mph (192 km/h) top speed, and an estimated weight of 485 lb (220 kg).

The analog analogy is spot on, with the display probably the simplest and most straightforward I’ve ever seen on an electric motorcycle. There’s also no app, no subscription, and no digital handcuffs. The bike is very much the electric equivalent of a simple ICE bike that just rides, albeit with a much nicer ride.

Unlike many of the futuristic concepts scattered around EICMA, ARES is actually headed toward limited production.

Real Motors plans to build just 250 examples in its first LOT 01 production run, with pricing starting at $20,000 and North American deliveries targeted for early 2027. European deliveries are expected after homologation is completed.

The tech giant has also brought former LiveWire CTO Vance Strader onto the project as it makes the difficult transition from a very cool prototype into an actual production motorcycle.

I actually had the chance to do a spin on the bike, and so I’ll be reporting back on the experience. But you can tell from my smile below that the ride was quite an experience!

Seatylock has been my go-to e-bike lock company for several years now, and I use their locks for my several e-bikes and my wife’s e-bike too.

Now Seatylock has returned with some even more impressive locks. The company highlighted off its new Ultra D28 lock, which is both angle grinder-proof and wide enough to lock the wheel of a motorcycle. It solves the problem of how do you make a lock strong enough for a motorcycle but also small and light enough that you can actually carry it with you, unlike a massive chain lock that usually stays where you park your motorcycle overnight.

In the image below, you can see the shackle next to an exposed section demonstrating the diamond coating that essentially destroys angle grinder discs – even diamond coated discs.

The company also has a slightly smaller version of the same lock designed for bicycles.

In a recent development, both will absolutely destroy even the toughest angle grinder discs. Sure, eventually someone could cut through them, but it may take a dozen discs and by that point the thief has moved on to an easier target.

At EICMA 2026, Royal Enfield continued expanding its electric motorcycle ambitions with its Flying Flea sub-brand, showcasing the scrambler-style motorcycle alongside its growing lineup of lightweight, retro-inspired electric motorcycles.

There were several interesting colorways and customized designs on display, showcasing the Flying Flea’s stylish design.

The new models blend Royal Enfield’s classic design heritage with modern electric technology, targeting urban riders and those looking for a fun, approachable electric motorcycle rather than a high-performance machine.

With distinctive styling, compact proportions, and an emphasis on accessible riding, the Flying Flea lineup represents Royal Enfield’s effort to carve out a place in the emerging market for smaller electric motorcycles while maintaining the character that has made its gasoline-powered bikes so popular.

Yamaha revealed off its newly introduced NMAX E electric scooter, bringing battery-powered performance to one of the brand’s most recognizable urban scooter families.

Designed as an electric alternative to the popular gasoline-powered NMAX, the upcoming model combines familiar sporty styling with a quiet, low-maintenance electric drivetrain aimed at everyday city commuting.

The NMAX E uses Yamaha’s latest compact eAxle powertrain, shared with the larger-wheeled XENTER E, and delivers up to 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power, putting it in the 125cc-equivalent class.

With its practical step-through design, automatic operation, and approachable performance, the NMAX E represents another step in Yamaha’s push to electrify its urban mobility lineup, particularly in European markets where scooters are already a popular alternative to cars.

Segway revealed off a newly introduced vision for safer electric scooters, including its futuristic X Cruiser concept that takes rider protection to a whole new level.

Rather than relying solely on traditional motorcycle safety equipment, the X Cruiser explores automotive-inspired features such as integrated seats with seatbelts, partial enclosures, and even a fully roofed version designed to offer additional protection from the elements.

The concept includes several configurations, ranging from a more conventional open scooter to a partially enclosed design and a fully covered model that looks like a cross between a motorcycle and a tiny electric car. While these designs are still concepts rather than production-ready scooters, they demonstrate how Segway is rethinking two-wheeled transportation by exploring ways to make electric scooters safer, more comfortable, and potentially more appealing to riders who might otherwise be hesitant to trade four wheels for two.

Eli Electric Vehicles took to EICMA 2026 to display its compact Eli Zero electric quadricycle, a tiny two-seat urban EV designed to offer much of the convenience of a car without the size, weight, or expense of a conventional automobile.

With its enclosed cabin, side-by-side seating, and ultra-compact footprint, the Eli Zero offers a practical alternative to larger vehicles for short city trips, combining the weather protection and comfort of a car with the maneuverability and efficiency of a much smaller vehicle.

It has been revealed that the company revealed a more powerful L7e-class version of the Eli Zero that it had previously teased, expanding the vehicle’s capabilities beyond its existing L6e configuration. The latest Race Edition also pushes the envelope farther with custom interior and a few extra accents to the body.

With growing interest in smaller, more efficient urban transportation, Eli’s presence at EICMA definitely underlined how the show is increasingly embracing electric mobility solutions that go beyond traditional motorcycles and scooters.

Industry observers note that NIU revealed off its latest lineup of electric scooters, continuing the brand’s push to make battery-powered two-wheelers a practical alternative to gasoline-powered urban transportation. Known for its sleek designs, connected technology, and approachable electric scooters, NIU highlighted models aimed at a range of riders, from everyday city commuters to those looking for more powerful machines capable of keeping up with faster urban traffic.

The company showed off several new models for the 2027 model year, with scooters that combine modern styling with features such as smartphone connectivity, smart security systems, and efficient electric drivetrains, all while maintaining the simplicity and low operating costs that make electric scooters so appealing.

While I didn’t see anything groundbreaking at the brand’s booth this year, the incremental updates look to push new tech features further throughout the brand’s many models, helping more of NIU’s offerings enter that premium level that the firm has been known for.

For something a bit wilder, Honda shared its futuristic EV Outlier Concept, an electric motorcycle that explores what two-wheeled design could look like when engineers are freed from the constraints of traditional gasoline-powered motorcycles.

In a recent development, with its long, low-slung profile, radically different riding position, and futuristic bodywork, the EV Outlier looks more like something out of a science fiction movie than a conventional motorcycle. The concept features electric motors integrated into both wheels, giving it two-wheel drive while opening up new possibilities for packaging and weight distribution.

Rather than simply replacing a combustion engine with a battery and motor, Honda used the EV Outlier to rethink the entire motorcycle layout, demonstrating how electrification could lead to entirely newly introduced types of riding experiences.

While the bike remains a design concept with no unveiled production looks, it offers an intriguing glimpse into Honda’s vision for the future of electric motorcycles.

Vespa demonstrated off its next-generation electric scooter lineup at EICMA, including electric versions of the Primavera, Sprint S, and Primavera Tech. While they don’t look radically different, there’s a lot more happening underneath the familiar steel bodywork.

A new Italian-made, rare-earth-free electric motor improves efficiency and performance, while the 45 km/h Primavera and Sprint S now feature removable batteries.

The faster 67 km/h Primavera Tech gets up to 90 km of WMTC range – a 12.5% improvement – along with an updated vehicle management system and more efficient charger.

#132765. Does Adversity Hurt Less the Second Time?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1023 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Does Adversity Hurt Less the Second Time?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Industry observers note that my grandfather owned a black World War II winter coat, long and heavy, the kind exhibitionists in movies wear, and in high school and college, I wore it everywhere because it reminded me of this sweet man who would watch Woody Woodpecker cartoons on television with me such that his laugh shook the bed.
  • Nietzsche wrote that what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger, so by his logic, I should have shrugged off my next problem easily.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Industry observers note that my grandfather owned a black World War II winter coat, long and heavy, the kind exhibitionists in movies wear, and in high school and college, I wore it everywhere because it reminded me of this sweet man who would watch Woody Woodpecker cartoons on television with me such that his laugh shook the bed. One night, outside a New York City bar, I realized it was too warm for wool and threw the coat back in my car. When my friends and I came back a few hours later, the window was broken in, and the thief took one thing: my grandfather’s coat.

Nietzsche wrote that what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger, so by his logic, I should have shrugged off my next problem easily. Three psychiatric researchers in Australia borrowed this overplayed line in the title of their scientific article, "What Doesn't Kill You Doesn't Always Make You Stronger: The Impact of Repeated Exposure to Adverse Life Events on Mental Health." Their work addresses questions taken for granted in a sloppy literature on resilience.

In a recent development, developmental psychologist Ann Masten coined the phrase that resilience is “ordinary magic” in 2001. It has since been dropped into commencement speeches and self-help books, usually shrunk down to the comforting idea that everyone has some. Masten’s own data say something far more precise. She spent years studying homeless families and described their reading and math grades:.

It has been revealed that our studies of homeless families have revealed striking variability within homeless populations, both in the degree of risk and also the level of competence or problems. For example, if one examines individual growth curves for children identified as homeless/highly mobile in the district, the variability becomes evident … Some children show consistent academic resilience, if one defines resilience as average or better reading or math achievement scores, whereas others show consistent problems, covering a range of 5 SD [five standard deviations] or more.

Industry observers note that variability means that some people experience amazing outcomes while others fall apart. Five standard deviations is a spread wide enough to stretch from the bottom 1 percent of the bell curve to the top 1 percent within a group of kids who all lack a stable bedroom. On average, homeless children scored below poor children who had housing, who in turn scored below children who were neither. Masten never stated resilience is a universal human endowment.

In a recent development, the myth of universal human resilience has a price. If most people bounce back on their own, the logical policy is to leave them alone. They will be fine... eventually.

It has been revealed that asking whether people are resilient is about as useful as asking whether people are tall, because the answer depends on who, measured against what, and when. The better question is what happens when you experience the same difficulty twice and whether the second hurts more or less than the first.

In a recent development, the Australian psychiatrists studied 23,109 adults who, between 2002 and 2023, experienced adversity. They looked at people who:.

Every year, the same people answered the same question: How much of the time during the past four weeks:.

Scores ran from 0 to 100, which let the researchers compare how far a person sank after a first challenge with how far the same person sank after a second.

Industry observers note that some might say the first time your finances blow up, you can blame bad luck, such as a crooked landlord. The second time, the explanation arrows start pointing at you.

Industry observers note that in the study, a first major financial loss lowered scores by 6 to 7 points, the steepest drop of the seven events. A second loss lowered them by 7 to 8 points, and a third hurt about as much as the second—so the harm grew, and then it leveled off.

According to recent reports, the people hit repeatedly were poorer to begin with, earning less before their first event. That is, the study revealed people with tough lives experience terrible events more often. It’s not exactly the most awe-inspiring finding, but it should make us more compassionate. My hypothesis is that a second financial loss comes after the savings account is empty, and you have already asked friends for a loan. By then, you feel incompetent and risk fraying your social ties.

A first theft or break-in lowered scores by about 1 point out of 100—the smallest effect in the study. By those stats, my coat should have been a shrug, and it wasn’t. A question about property crime can’t distinguish a stolen car stereo from my grandfather’s WWII coat. The authors close their paper with the same mentality, arguing that how much an event hurts depends on what the lost thing means to the person and how much is in their psychological arsenal to absorb the pain.

Divorce and serious personal illness or injury both did less harm the second time, so some might offer advice that your second divorce will sting less. As a divorced man, I’m in no hurry to find out, and you shouldn’t either.

A smaller mental health reaction can also mean a person stopped feeling much. For instance, people assaulted three or more times reacted less to each upcoming attack, and 64 percent of them were women, which unfortunately we know is often a sign of domestic violence.

I want to warn you and everyone you know that emotional numbing should not be misunderstood as resilience or growth.

Sources indicate that so did losing my grandpa’s coat make me stronger? Not in the slightest. It was an isolated experience that pissed me off. You, too, have similar one-offs that do not fit tidy little psychological models. Do not assume resilience or breakdowns. Pay attention, ask questions, and listen to better understand the person beside you.

WHOEVER STATED PATIENCE is a virtue did not have facial hair, or at least, they weren’t regularly shaving it. Of course, there are plenty of reasons punctual guys might want to use an electric razor in lieu of traditional cartridge razors. These shavers are gentler on skin, gliding across the face with less direct blade contact to reduce irritation and minimize the risk of nicks and cuts. They also help prevent razor bumps and burns by trimming hair above the surface instead of dragging against the skin like traditional razors do.

It has been revealed that to be clear, it takes skin a few sessions to get used to shaving with these devices if you’ve been a long-time cartridge devotee. This is because electric razors move differently and do not cut as close, so your skin needs time to adapt to the upcoming sensation and technique. Also, switching razors changes how the blades interact with your skin, which can cause temporary irritation as your skin builds tolerance.

In a recent development, still, these tools streamline the whole process: they're fast, easy to use, and travel-friendly since you don’t need to pack extra products, like shaving cream. Many models even come with smart features like pressure sensors and AI, making them more intuitive and unique to the user. Most you can use wet or dry, with or without shaving cream, and they're versatile enough for your face, head, or body. Plus, some have add-ons that can help you replace multiple grooming tools, simplify your routine, and free up space on your bathroom shelf.

Industry observers note that the blade type is a key factor to consider when choosing an electric razor. You’ll typically choose between two main options: rotary blades and foil blades.

If you usually let your stubble grow out or don’t shave every day, a rotary electric razor is your best bet. Its circular motion and flexible head follow the curves of your face, helping it cut through longer or more uneven hair with ease. Rotary razors work especially well for those with normal to tougher skin and medium to coarse beard density, offering a comfortable and efficient shave even after a few days of growth.

It has been revealed that A foil works best for shorter facial hair or when you're aiming for a close shave similar to classic razors. It uses oscillating blades hidden beneath a thin, perforated foil that captures and cuts hairs as they emerge through the mesh. While a foil shaver tends to be noisier than rotary models, it offers deeper precision. To get the smoothest results, use it with straight, steady strokes—moving back and forth along the face and neck. This design makes foil razors ideal for those who shave daily or want clean, sharp lines around facial hair.

Corded razors plug directly into a power source, so you don’t have to worry about charging or replacing batteries. As a result, they deliver more consistent power and longer performance. Since they don’t need to conserve energy, they also usually run stronger than cordless models. That mentioned, cordless razors offer added convenience, especially for travel or grooming on the go, with options powered by either rechargeable or disposable batteries. Ultimately, the right choice depends on your routine and how much flexibility you need.

The Men’s Health grooming team has been extensively testing electric razors since 2018. For years, we’ve been putting shavers to the test, evaluating their effectiveness, durability, and ease of use over long periods of time. As someone who can get a five o'clock shadow before lunch, I am constantly shaving. This has given me a consistent canvas to test and retest editor favorites, as well as the latest innovations and upcoming grooming releases.

Recent findings suggest that for this story, I considered the team’s reviews and notes of top-performing razors dating back eight years, in addition to my own experience, to land on 15 options to extensively test or retest over an 18-month trial period. I’ve also included before-and-after shots of yours truly for most of the razors to show the kind of shave each one delivers. Based on this first-hand use, I narrowed that list to eight, representing the best electric razors for men to buy in 2026.

Sources indicate that both electric and manual razors use blades to cut hair, but they do it in different ways. Manual razors pull each hair up with the first blade, then slice it closer to the skin with the following blades—kind of like using a knife. Electric razors, on the other hand, work more like scissors. Most use a foil system: hair enters tiny holes in the foil, and internal blades cut it from beneath. Rotary versions use a slightly different mechanism, but the concept is similar.

Industry observers note that manual razors shave closer because the blades touch the skin directly. That closeness comes with a downside: higher chances of razor burn, bumps, or ingrown hairs, especially if you skip proper prep or use a dull blade. Electric razors always have a barrier between the blade and skin, so while they won’t shave quite as close, they’re often gentler and better suited for sensitive skin.

According to recent reports, using an electric razor is much easier to pick up compared to a traditional or safety razor. Still, don’t just grab yours and start shaving right away. Take the time to learn how to get the closest shave possible before speeding through the process for the best results.

Start your shave with clean skin. Whether you’re using a wet or dry shaver, you should tackle your scruff right after washing your face. For dry shavers, apply a small amount of pre-shave oil or wash your face and then gently pat it dry. These shavers perform best when the stubble is firm and completely dry.

It has been revealed that keep the razor at a 90-degree angle to your skin to avoid cutting hairs unevenly. There’s no need to press hard, as a light grip does the job. Pressing down too much, especially around the jaw or chin, can lead to patchy results and irritation. With a foil shaver, I stick to back-and-forth strokes. If I’m using a rotary, I’ll go with either circular or straight motions, depending on what feels best.

In a recent development, reading the manual might seem unnecessary (and boring), but brands often include specific tips or techniques tailored to their design. Those little details can make a significant difference, resulting in a noticeably smoother shave. It might not be Hemingway, but taking a few minutes to go through the instructions usually pays off in better results and a more comfortable experience overall.

Recent findings suggest that as long as I stick to proper maintenance and care, I get a consistently smooth shave from electric razors. If you’re upcoming to these tools, however, give your skin about two weeks to adjust—it makes a significant difference. A little patience and upkeep go a long way.

Recent findings suggest that one of the first things I check in an electric razor is how easy it is to clean because this will help both its effectiveness and longevity (not to mention my blood pressure). Skipping regular cleaning can clog the blades with hair and gunk, which not only affects performance but also shortens the razor’s life. When using a waterproof device, I always rinse mine under running water after each use, then use a small brush to clear out any buildup on the foil.

Industry observers note that that foil is key to getting a smooth, even shave, but it’s delicate. If it gets bent or damaged, replace it right away. Letting it go risks rough shaves, irritation, or even breakouts from dragging dirt across your skin. Some higher-end models, like the Braun Series 9, come with automatic cleaning stations. They’re super convenient (even if a bit bulky and noisy) and use replaceable cartridges that last around three months—about $5 each in a multi-pack. While not essential, they definitely make it easier to stay on top of maintenance.

Read More: How To Maintain Your Beard Trimmer.

High-quality electric razors—especially those in the $200-plus range—can last years, sometimes even five or more if well maintained. To keep mine running strong, I make sure to replace the blades and foil regularly. Depending on the brand, blade replacement is usually recommended every 6 to 18 months. I also keep an eye on the foil. If it gets dented or damaged, I swap it out immediately since most replacement cartridges include both parts.

It has been revealed that these typically cost between $20 and $50. Battery life is typically the first thing to go. Over time, even the best razors start to lose their charge faster or run with less power. When I notice my shave isn’t as close, or the razor starts pulling instead of cutting cleanly, that’s my cue that it might be time for a new one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai is skipping the typical mid-cycle refresh and prepares to launch a completely redesigned Kona, with a sleek newly introduced style and an updated high-tech interior.

It’s been nearly four years since Hyundai introduced the second-generation Kona, meaning, like most of its models, the compact SUV was expected to receive a mid-cycle refresh.

Recent findings suggest that hyundai is apparently going straight to the third-generation model instead. Earlier this year, early-stage prototypes were spotted in Korea that looked much boxier and more rugged than the current Kona.

Since then, several test mules have been captured testing in the US, Europe, and other regions, confirming the Kona will adopt a more upright, traditional SUV design similar to the fresh Santa Fe, Palisade, and Tucson.

The wider, more powerful design appears to draw inspiration from Hyundai’s off-road Crater Concept, revealed at the LA Auto Show last year.

Hyundai noted the off-road SUV Concept was a preview of the “next evolution” of its Extreme Rugged Terrain (XRT) vehicles, such as the IONIQ 5 XRT and Palisade XRT Pro. Is the Kona next in line to receive the XRT treatment?

A post shared by SHORTS CAR (@shorts_car).

Apparent leaked images from a few months ago revealed a design that looked like a mashup of the Crater Concept and IONIQ 5, with pixelated lighting and a clamshell hood.

Most recently, the third-gen Hyundai Kona, codenamed “SX3,” was spotted disguised in a parking garage in Korea. The images were sent to ShortsCar, revealing the new Kona’s wheel design.

While earlier reports suggested Hyundai planned to drop the all-electric Kona variant and would only offer gas and hybrid versions, the prototype captured in Korea is expected to be the EV model. However, Hyundai has yet to confirm powertrain or battery specs.

The updates are even more evident on the inside. Previous spy images appeared to show the third-gen Hyundai Kona running Hyundai’s latest Pleos Connect infotainment system, like the IONIQ 3.

In the IONIQ 3, Hyundai offers a 12.9″ or 14.6″ center infotainment screen, plus an optional driver display.

Like the current model, the third-gen Kona is expected to be available with fully electric (EV), hybrid, and gas-powered powertrains.

While Hyundai skipped the 2026 Kona EV, the electric version could return in 2027 or 2028 when the third-generation model is expected to arrive.

The hybrid version will likely use the same 1.6L hybrid engine as the latest Seltos, while the EV variant could offer similar powertrain and battery options to the IONIQ 3.

The IONIQ 3 is available with two battery packs in Europe and the UK: 42 kWh and 61 kWh, offering WLTP ranges of up to 213 miles (344 km) and 308 miles (497 km), respectively.

Get the Women’s Health Beginner Workout Plan: 4-Week Strength Training and Cardio Program

📅 23 Feb 2023 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s not just you—everyone really is starting to work out lately.
  • It has been revealed that so, if that’s you, let me officially say welcome to the party.
  • According to recent reports, the Women’s Health+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Proposal takes the guesswork out of starting your fitness journey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s not just you—everyone really is starting to work out lately. My feed is full of people hitting the weights for the first time ever or setting major goals like getting their first pull-up. And let me just say: It’s awesome!

It has been revealed that so, if that’s you, let me officially say welcome to the party. When you’re starting to work out, it can be hard to sift through all the options and find a program that’s actually accessible for a true beginner (or, someone restarting after quite some time). That is, until now.

According to recent reports, the Women’s Health+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Proposal takes the guesswork out of starting your fitness journey. This comprehensive program guides you through strength and cardio workouts that only take between 20 and 45 minutes. And, of course, it answers every burning question you could have about starting a fitness routine.

No matter your age or experience, starting an exercise routine has many benefits, states Kristen McParland, CPT, your coach for the next four weeks. Building muscle increases total-body strength; your bones, ligaments, and tendons get healthier; and even your blood pressure and immunity may improve. So lace up those sneakers and we’ll see you at the gym now, too.

Download the WH+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Initiative.

Over the next four weeks, you’ll follow a specific proposal each day, focusing either on strength training, optional cardio, active recovery, or rest (more on these, below). Each strength workout includes a warm-up and a cooldown (which you can use on cardio days, too). More info on each below.

According to recent reports, simply follow the instructions of each full-body strength training workout in the Women's Health+ Beginner Workout Plan. You can find detailed how-to instructions for each exercise in the Exercise Guide section of the PDF.

Equipment Needed: Dumbbells, kettlebells, a step or box, and a slam ball. Don’t have access to a kettlebell or slam ball? Don't worry—you can still do those exercises with a dumbbell.

In a recent development, cardio is vital for everyone, regardless of fitness level or routine. That’s because when you’re lifting heavy, your heart needs to be able to take on that stress. Training cardio—through running, cycling, or brisk walking—will help improve your heart strength.

If you’re a beginner when it comes to cardio, simply start at your own pace and build. Complete 20 to 30 minutes of running, biking, cycling, rowing, or using the elliptical or stair climber (whatever you enjoy). No matter which form of cardio you choose, start with interval training: exert yourself for 30 seconds, then go at a light pace for 1 to 2 minutes, alternating the pattern for a total of 20 minutes. The goal is to “get your heart rate up, but then pull it back and recover,” McParland says. Eventually, you’ll be able to decrease the rest time and maintain that higher-intensity movement for 15 to 20 minutes without a break.

Your activity on this day is up to you. The goal is to do some kind of low-intensity movement lasting 20 minutes. Some ideas: outdoor walk or hike, bike ride, incline treadmill walk, yoga, or Pilates class.

Take this day to relax so your muscles have time to repair. Still, if your body is craving some type of activity for recovery, you could stretch, go for a walk, or even try a treatment like a massage, sauna, or cold-plunge session.

Here’s how things will progress each week.

Complete the five programmed workouts when it’s convenient for you. Focus on your form and take your two rest days when you need to recover.

It has been revealed that if you completed all the workouts in Week 1, repeat them during Week 2, adjusting one variable in your routine, McParland states: the number of reps or sets, the weight, the speed of the moves (slower is harder). If you missed a workout, don’t stress. Refocus on completing all of the Week 1 workouts before making any of the changes above.

You’ve officially done two full weeks of this workout strategy—nice job! During this third week, repeat the workouts from Week 2 in exactly the same way or adjust one variable again (reps or sets, weight, range of motion, speed, and rest periods). If you feel you’re crushing it and are ready to level up, try the third full-body strength workout.

Recent findings suggest that still going strong? Thought so! Hit all six workouts and adjust one variable per workout for an extra challenge (reps or sets, weight, range of motion, speed, rest time). You can also ramp up your cardio time (to 30 to 40 minutes) or speed, shorten rest intervals (for interval training), or raise your step goal by 10 percent (e.g., if your daily step goal was 5,000 a day, make it 5,500).

According to recent reports, ready to become your strongest self? Download the WH+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan now.

Sources indicate that when you’re just beginning to work out, do a minimum of two full-body strength training days each week, McParland recommends. During both of those days, you should hit at least one exercise from each category of the foundational movement patterns. This will give you enough of a challenge to stimulate muscle growth, she states.

During the first two weeks of this blueprint, you will have two strength training days per week (each session will run 36 to 43 minutes), two optional cardio/step days per week (each session will 20 to 30 minutes), one day of active rest (a stint of low-intensity movement lasting at least 20 minutes), and two recovery days, for a total of five workouts per week.

After those two weeks, see how your body feels and if your body is craving a third day of full-body training. If so, progress to the next phase of this blueprint. That weekly schedule consists of three strength training days per week (each session will run 36 to 43 minutes), two optional cardio/step days per week (each session will run 20 to 30 minutes), one active rest day (lasting at least 20 minutes), and one recovery day, for a total of six workouts per week. If your body isn’t ready for three strength-training days yet, wait another two weeks. Once you’ve completed the full four weeks of this plan, consider adding in the third day.

What kind of weights should I choose?

Sources indicate that start with medium weights that will challenge you for 10 to 12 reps, indicates Sariya. Essentially, you’ll want to feel you’ve reached 70 to 80 percent of your rate of perceived exertion (i.e., your fatigue level is at a 7 or 8 out of 10) by the time you’re doing your final reps in a set. When you feel you can do more than 12 reps, it’s time to increase your weight, but keep the same number of reps. This way, you’re always working toward your goal of building strength.

As for how much to increase by: a good rule of thumb is 2.5 to 5 pounds for an upper-body exercise and 5 to 10 pounds for a lower-body move.

What if I need to rest in the middle of a set?

Resting during a workout is important—if you don’t take enough time to recover between exercises, you won’t have enough energy in your body for the next one. With this proposal, you’ll rest between moves in a superset or tri-set for 20 to 30 seconds, or however long it takes to transition between exercises. Between supersets and tri-sets, you’ll rest for one minute.

If you get fatigued in the middle of a set, push through if you feel safe doing so, Sariya states. However, if you feel dizzy or fear you might drop a weight on yourself, put it down and take time to recover. When you’re feeling better, you can start again. If you’re in any sort of pain, stop the workout entirely.

What kind of cardio should I do?

Cardio is a great supplement to strength training, McParland notes. Plus, it has a slew of benefits, such as better endurance in strength training, better blood pressure regulation, and higher VO2 max, she says.

If you’re a beginner when it comes to cardio, simply start at your own pace and build. Pick any form of cardio you enjoy, whether that’s brisk walking, running, cycling, or swimming, and sprinkle it in two or three days a week for 20 to 30 minutes, McParland recommends.

What should I do on recovery days?

On an active rest day, you’ll still exercise a bit through low-intensity movement, like a leisurely bike ride or hike. On a recovery day, you’ll do just that: recover. After all, you need to give your muscles time to rebuild and repair, Sariya notes. But to maximize the recovery aspect, you can also opt to stretch, go for a gentle walk, or even get a self-care body treatment like a massage.

Once you’ve got the WH+ Beginner Workout Plan under your belt, you’re ready to take things to another level. One way to do that is by simply restarting the program—and completing the moves with heavier weights this time. (This is called progressive overload, and it’s another foundational concept in strength training. The idea is that over time, you will keep increasing the stimulus to your muscles to continuously challenge them and make them stronger.).

Picking the right weight is an art as much as it is a science, but for a general rule of thumb, for upper-body moves, increase your weights by 2.5 to 5 pounds and see how that feels. For lower-body ones, try adding 5 to 10. You should feel like you’re ending each set two to three reps away from failure (where your form starts to break down). You can tell you’re close if your range of motion starts to shorten or your reps are slowing down. That’s how you know you’re successfully challenging yourself. And, if you don’t happen to have a lot of different-sized weights at your disposal, you can always just increase the number of reps you do instead.

But, if you’re looking for something new, WH+ has a bunch of other trainer-created programs to help you grow your knowledge and confidence in the gym and attack other fitness goals.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A classic BMW 2002 is a simple, mechanical machine.
  • Industry observers note that according to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recall report, BMW is recalling 286 i5 and i7 electric sedans in the United States because some vehicles may have been equipped with testing software, instead of the production software intended to manage high-voltage battery charging.
  • The recall includes 236 examples of the 2026–2027 BMW i5, including the eDrive40, xDrive40, and M60 variants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A classic BMW 2002 is a simple, mechanical machine. However, a modern BMW sedan is a rolling computer, one that relies heavily on software. And when that software is buggy, challenges can arise—which is why the software is tested extensively before going to production. But what happens when that test software mistakenly makes it into production cars?

Industry observers note that according to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recall report, BMW is recalling 286 i5 and i7 electric sedans in the United States because some vehicles may have been equipped with testing software, instead of the production software intended to manage high-voltage battery charging. In rare cases, this could expose people to a higher risk of an electric shock.

The recall includes 236 examples of the 2026–2027 BMW i5, including the eDrive40, xDrive40, and M60 variants. Another 50 vehicles are 2027 BMW i7 50 xDrive and 60 xDrive models. All the affected vehicles were manufactured between May and July 2026.

BMW first became aware of the issue on October 8, 2026, when high-voltage battery charging port supplier TE Connectivity Solutions GmbH alerted the automaker. An investigation ensued, and it was discovered that some charging units were mistakenly shipped with test software instead of production software. BMW is not aware of any injuries or accidents related to this problem.

Sources indicate that no hardware changes are required to rectify the glitch, and the affected vehicles will require a software enhancement. The recall report does not specify that this can be fixed via an over-the-air update, so a trip to the dealer will likely be required.

BMW looks to mail owner notification letters beginning December 25, 2026, although we doubt the U.S.P.S. will be doing much picking up or delivery that day. Starting that same date, owners can also check their vehicle's recall status through the NHTSA recall website by using their VIN, but we suggest waiting until after the kids are done opening presents.

Tesla stops selling every Cybertruck except the $109,990 Cyberbeast

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.
  • In a recent development, the Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected.
  • Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator shows today with a Los Angeles delivery address:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.

In a recent development, the Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected. So the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today costs $109,990, up 57% from $69,990 in early August.

Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator shows today with a Los Angeles delivery address:.

A week ago, the Cyberbeast cost $102,490. Before that, it was $99,990. That’s a $10,000 (10%) increase in about a week on a truck that hasn’t changed: 320 miles of estimated range, 11,000 lbs of towing, and 0-60 mph in 2.6 seconds.

Sources indicate that on November 6, the same day Elon Musk announced the end of Cybertruck production, Tesla raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. That made the $92,490 Premium AWD the entry point. Now it’s gone too, with no announcement. The configurator just stopped letting you pick it.

Upcoming inventory isn’t an alternative either. When we checked, Tesla’s inventory search showed no new Cybertrucks within 200 miles of Los Angeles.

This comes two days after Musk extended Cybertruck production through the end of summer 2027 to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” On Monday, he claimed the order rate “far exceeds” production and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.”.

Sources indicate that if there really is a backlog, cutting off the two cheaper trims is one way to cap it before the line shuts down. It also pushes whatever demand is left toward the most expensive, highest-margin version of the truck.

Industry observers note that but the sales data doesn’t describe a truck with a demand problem in the other direction. We estimate Tesla delivered 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks in Q3, a pace of about 30,000 a year on a line with more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. And in February, Tesla was offering a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 for “only the next 10 days.”.

It has been revealed that that’s $50,000 less than the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today. Nine months later.

According to recent reports, some of those $59,990 buyers are still waiting on delivery dates pushed into 2027. Tesla hasn’t stated whether their orders, or any other Dual Motor and Premium orders in the queue, will be built before production ends.

Unlike the thousands of $59k CT orders that may never get manufactured I can guarantee that every high margin $110k CyberBeast order will be delivered before production ends.

According to recent reports, this is the wind-down playbook, and it’s moving faster than I expected. Announce the end, raise prices, pull the cheaper trims, and sell the last trucks in their most expensive form. Tesla is squeezing as much as it can out of every remaining Cybertruck.

Industry observers note that I don’t blame Tesla for wanting margin on a program it’s walking away from. But it makes the “order backlog” talk look like what we noted it was: an end-of-life rush Tesla created by announcing the end, now being monetized with a $109,990 sticker. Not great for anyone who was told in 2019 that this truck would start at $39,900, or that the tri-motor version would cost $69,900.

If you want a Cybertruck that isn’t a Cyberbeast, you’re now shopping used. And I’d keep an eye on used prices, because a truck that’s going out of production with no cheaper new option could hold its value better than it has over the last two years.

In the Berkshires, an Intensely Yellow Kitchen Is Anything but Mellow in This Lakeside Cottage
