💡 Key Takeaways
  • I DIDN’T START out as a “boot guy.” I always thought they were clunky, poorly stitched and didn’t provide enough insole support like my favorite Nike Air Force 1s.
  • Since then, the Men’s Health style team and I have tested well over 50 pairs across every silhouette imaginable: cowboy boots, hiking boots, waterproof commuters, dressier Chelsea styles, heritage work boots—the whole lineup.
  • Recent findings suggest that the iconic Blundstone #585 still reigns supreme for its comfort, durability, and style.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I DIDN’T START out as a “boot guy.” I always thought they were clunky, poorly stitched and didn’t provide enough insole support like my favorite Nike Air Force 1s. But 15 years ago, I bought my first pair of Timberland 6-Inch Premium Boots because a brutal winter hit the East Coast, and slipping around in sneakers wasn’t going to cut it. I needed something that could survive the rain, snow, and slush. It didn’t take long to realize that once fall hits, having a solid pair (or two) in rotation is a non-negotiable. That first leather lace-up carried me through snowball fights and more than a few questionable bar floors—and it sold me on what a good boot can do.

Since then, the Men’s Health style team and I have tested well over 50 pairs across every silhouette imaginable: cowboy boots, hiking boots, waterproof commuters, dressier Chelsea styles, heritage work boots—the whole lineup. I’ve worn them on shoots, to weddings, on rainy office days, and on long travel runs, and I can confirm: not every boot is bulky. The right pair can feel as clean and sleek as your favorite sneakers. So if you’re looking for something versatile enough to move from the office to the bar or carry you from one event to the next, we’ve got you covered. Our picks deliver comfort, durability, and style, whether you need a tough trail option, something practical for wet commutes, or a sleek pair for a night out.

Recent findings suggest that the iconic Blundstone #585 still reigns supreme for its comfort, durability, and style. Part Chelsea boot, part work boot, its leather feels soft with a pre-distressed texture, while inside is cushy and snug from the moment you put it on. We didn’t feel any tightness or have to wait a couple of wears for it to mold to our feet. Our editor Tim Kohut wears it at his standing desk for seven hours straight, and his feet never give in or develop blisters. He even took it on a weekend hike and felt comfortable the whole way, hills, dips, and all. The pull tabs also make it easy to slide your foot in and out.

Sources indicate that I’ve worn warmer boots in my testing, but they were much bulkier. This pair has a lighter, slimmer build, yet works for general fall and winter gear. The boot’s leather upper dries in minutes, whether I get caught in light showers or trudge through three inches of snow. Yes, the material can scuff if you’re not careful, but a quick wipe with a damp cloth brings it right back. After months of near-daily wear, the elastic panels haven’t stretched out, the sole hasn’t flattened, and the leather has developed a natural patina versus looking beat up. Underfoot, the synthetic polyurethane midsole feels like a thick layer of cushioning, softening every step, especially on Latest York’s uneven sidewalks.

In a recent development, in the toe area, my feet have wiggle room instead of feeling cramped. Whether for style or performance, this boot works in a variety of settings. I’ve worn mine with a sweater and dark denim for dinner as well as chinos for the office, and it pairs seamlessly with any casual staples like a flannel overshirt, tee, and jeans under a fall jacket. The price tag may give you pause, but most boots that I’ve spent over $100 on are worth it. You don’t have to baby this one. It looks good as new after being worn everywhere, so it’s a reliable option for work, travel, and trail.

Read More: Blundstone 585 Chelsea Boot Review.

When our senior fitness and commerce editor Brett Williams slipped into the Beckett Simonon Bolton Chelsea, he immediately called out how sharp it looked. This Chelsea boot—a style originating in 19th-century Britain as a close-fitting riding boot with elastic side panels—elevates whatever you’re wearing. The super premium, full-grain calfskin leather has a natural sheen and structure, and the almond-shaped toe box gives it a sleek profile that reads dressy. Inside, the Vachetta leather lining helped keep his foot cool and surprisingly comfortable after hours at his standing desk.

Brett wore it with suits, dress pants, and black denim on shoot days, and it held up across the board. And yes, Chelseas aren’t strictly “formal only” anymore, but the Bolton proves that a dress-leaning Chelsea can still be incredibly versatile. The stitched construction makes it lighter and more flexible than the typical Goodyear-welted options. It’s easily one of the best leather Chelsea boots on the market because it nails every detail: premium calfskin, a breathable lining, a sleek silhouette, and real comfort. Plenty of Chelseas look the part but feel clunky or overly stiff, so the $279 is justifiable.

Read More: Best Chelsea Boots for Men.

According to recent reports, our grooming editor, Sean Zucker, took the Amberjack Chukka for a proper test run, and he came back raving about how wildly comfortable it felt from the jump. The full-grain leather upper and sheepskin lining give it a polished look, but the real magic is underfoot: the heat-activated insole that molds to your feet after a few wears. Plus, the lightweight outsole feels closer to a cushy sneaker than a traditional boot.

According to recent reports, sean wore it on rainy commutes, into the office, and around the city on weekend errands. He didn’t have any sore arches or slips on wet sidewalks. The leather ages nicely over time, and the overall vibe lands squarely in that “smart casual” sweet spot. It works with chinos and slim trousers, and can stretch to dark denim, but it’s not meant to stand in for a dress boot.

Industry observers note that if you’ve dismissed cowboy boots as too costumey, Tecovas offers a sleek option that balances rugged style and pairs with a bunch of casual and dressy fits. The round-toe design features a tough, beautiful cowhide leather that wears well whether you’re dressing up or down. The cowhide leather gives the Cartwright a durable feel, while its classic round toe and signature stitching keep the design recognizable.

In a recent development, surprisingly, I didn’t have to break this boot in. From the first wear, it felt comfortable without any pinching or stiffness. To coincide with the theme, I wore it to Beyoncé’s Cowboy Carter concert in Fresh Jersey, and I stood the entire three hours. During the first half of the show, it started lightly raining, but the leather dried in seconds. While it’s not as grippy on slippery surfaces as the Merrell and Timberland boots, it’s stable enough for most city sidewalks. Our editors found it to be suitable for the office, the bar, or even a wedding. It’s one of those boots that you can wear year-round. Tecovas offers a few different colors, but we’re especially into the hazelnut, which looks great with dark jeans or dressier pants.

In a recent development, what really makes this Tecovas pair stand out is how approachable it feels, especially if you’ve never owned a cowboy boot before. The 12-inch shaft—the part of the boot that rises from your ankle to your lower calf—isn’t overly tall or stiff, so it slips easily under straight or relaxed-fit jeans. Also, the 1½-inch heel is low and manageable, so you get a classic cowboy shape without feeling like you’re walking on a block. Fit-wise, it runs true to size and feels secure without squeezing the instep, which is often the biggest concern with Western-style boots. If you want the look without committing to something flashy or trend-driven, this is a smart, low-risk entry point that still feels elevated.

Timberland’s classic work boot has outlasted trendy styles for decades because it’s durable, has a timeless design, and goes with everything. Aptly named the “Butters”, it’s one of the most recognizable boots because of its signature cut and proportions: the high top, thick lug sole, and warm wheat-colored nubuck leather. It’s become a staple across music, streetwear and sports culture. I’ve had it in rotation since I was a teen and still weave it into my casual fits to this day. Yes, it takes one to three wears to break in, but after that you get a snug, customized fit that you can fine-tune with the laces.

The Timberland boot’s cultural relevance hasn’t slowed down, either. A lot of fashion gents like Timothée Chalamet have been spotted wearing Timberland off-duty and even at red carpet events. It also taps into today’s men’s trends, especially the ongoing ’90s-Y2K revival, where baggier denim, boxy jackets, and easy, layered knits are back in rotation.

This boot has full-grain and nubuck leather uppers that can handle scuffs and are fully waterproof, so rain and slush never ruin the look. It's sturdier and heavier than most fashion boots, because it was originally built for work, but it doesn't feel like you’re lugging around bricks all day. The bulk is part of the style, and why it pairs so well with relaxed denim, cargos, and winter fits. Whether I’m walking on wet sidewalks or cobblestone, the lug sole feels stable underfoot.

Recent findings suggest that if we’re judging purely on trail performance, the Merrell Thermo Chill 2 is the best pick for hiking. The mid-height design gives your ankles the extra support they need on uneven terrain, so you’re not wobbling around. Most hiking boot outsoles rely on standard rubber compounds that work well, but they usually sacrifice grip for durability or flexibility. With 200g insulation, this style makes for a perfect winter boot.

Sources indicate that it’s fully waterproof, so puddles, rain, or soggy grass aren’t going to slow you down. The main draw here is the exclusive footbed, which molds to your foot, over time, giving each step a cushioned, natural feel. Brower wore this boot on a weekend camping trip, splashing through soggy trails and wet grass, and by the end of it, his feet were dry and comfortable. The mesh on the tongue keeps things breathable, too, so when the sun comes out, your feet don’t feel like they’re baking. While it’s not as sleek as the Danner boot, it’s still a solid-looking boot that you can wear off the trail.

Recent findings suggest that most rugged boots are kind of ugly, but Danner delivers a trail-ready option that actually looks sharp. The rich tan color paired with red laces gives it a bold yet unique look for the trail. Outside of hikes, our Tech and Gear editor Ryan Brower likes to style it with a flannel shirt and jeans. He’s been wearing it consistently over the last couple fall seasons. It’s not the warmest option in freezing 30-degree temps, so it might be wise to wear with thicker socks. It’s made with full-grain leather uppers, which age beautifully and bead off rain. Plus, the waterproof liners keep water from getting inside.

Full-grain leather is also tougher and more durable than corrected grain or split leather (found in cheaper boots) that have been sanded or split down, losing their outer layers. The break-in period takes a little patience, but after a few wears, this boot feels comfortable and natural. The Vibram outsole grips especially well on uneven terrain, whether you’re climbing trails in the Oregon mountains or navigating slick city streets in Fresh York. Between the outsole and insole, there’s a fiberglass shank—a thin, supportive layer that reinforces the midfoot. It helps keep your feet stable, prevents the boot from twisting, and reduces fatigue on long walks.

Red Wing has been crafting durable, American-made workwear for more than a century, supplying tradesmen, factory workers and miners with boots built to last. The Classic Moc Boot continues that tradition with a roomy moc toe, weatherproof leather construction, and a comfortable wedge sole that makes long hours on your feet far more manageable. (A moc toe is a stitched toe design where the seam wraps around the front of the boot, giving extra room and durability.).

In a recent development, men’s Health designer Jason Speakman broke it in on a hike in upstate Upcoming York. Since the leather is a bit hefty, it did take some getting used to. But after about two or three wears, he mentioned it didn’t feel as cramped as other moc toe boots he's tested. There was no strain on his feet after going from rocks to packed trails, and they stayed comfortable even on uneven terrain. Aesthetically, it has the rugged, All-American vibe that works on a job site, weekend trail, or just rolling up to the beer hall in jeans. The full-grain oiled leather is super premium, so this option will last years and develop a cool, worn-in patina.

After doing some work in the yard for hours on end, Speakman found the EVA midsole—which is a foam material that’s both lightweight and strong—makes this boot the most comfortable option for raking leaves and pushing a lawnmower. It also handles hard surfaces like concrete or brick, keeping your feet cushioned and protected from constant pounding.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for a hiking boot that won’t make your wallet flinch but still performs like something far more expensive, the Nortiv8’s offering is an easy win. On the trail it proved, while affordable, that it’s not cheaply made. Right out of the box, the waterproof synthetic leather and textile upper felt surprisingly substantial—not floppy or flimsy like some lower-cost boots. The material stood up to brush and rocks on a muddy forest loop, and after hours of hauling gear and setting up camp in wet grass, it still looked crisp with no signs of fraying.

The waterproof membrane lived up to its promise during shallow creek crossings and soggy morning hikes; my socks stayed dry every time, even when water pooled around my feet. Underfoot, the rubber lug outsole delivered dependable traction. I tested it while fishing and the grip felt stable and sturdy. The midsole’s cushioned EVA foam struck a nice balance too: supportive on long miles but soft enough that my feet didn’t feel trashed by day’s end. It’s not an ultralight trail runner, but for hiking, camping, fishing, and general outdoor wear, the way these materials work together is impressive for the price.

Not many boots can pull off a tailored suit, but Frye’s luxe ankle style is the rare exception. I’ve been wearing mine for the past couple months, and it instantly makes any semi-formal fit feel sharper. The design is simple but polished with a premium leather upper and is stitched around the edge for extra durability. I wore it in light rain and the material dried in seconds. I also found the inner-side zipper makes life so much easier when I’m slipping it on and off after a long day. It was refreshing that it didn’t require an annoying break-in period. When I first tried it on, I realized I had wiggle room in the toe area right away.

Recent findings suggest that after five wears, the leather starts to crease naturally, but that adds personality to the boot without it looking worn. I’ve tested it on city streets and light rain, and the grip is solid enough to feel confident walking anywhere without slipping or scuffing the leather. The ankle height is flattering, the shape is not heavy-looking, and the richness of the leather colors pairs with different outfits. You can rock jeans and a sweater for a casual lunch, or dress it up with slacks and a blazer.

Sure, this boot isn’t cheap, but the quality, durability, and timeless design make it worth the investment. You’re paying for a boot that will remain in good condition for years, look better as it ages, and feel comfortable from day one.

Leather is a reliable choice for everyday boots because it can be durable and develop character with wear. Full-grain and nubuck each have their own look and feel, but neither guarantees waterproof protection on its own. If you’re regularly walking through rain or slush, look for a waterproof membrane or specifically waterproof construction.

Recent findings suggest that EVA foam midsoles are lightweight and cushioned, perfect for long days on your feet. Some boots use polyurethane midsoles, which are a bit heavier but offer more durability and stability, especially if you’re on rugged terrain.

It has been revealed that your traction and durability depend on this part. Vibram outsoles are often considered the gold standard for their grip and long-lasting wear. Rubber outsoles are common on everyday and outdoor boots because they can provide traction and abrasion resistance. Grip varies by rubber compound and tread pattern, so look for an outsole designed for the surfaces and conditions you’ll encounter.

It has been revealed that goodyear-welted boots can be a good investment because their construction often allows the outsole to be replaced when it wears down. The welt can also help limit water intrusion, although the construction alone doesn’t make a boot waterproof.

Our fashion team, led by longtime boots enthusiast and Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, found the most comfortable and durable options out there. We put more than 50 pairs of boots through the wringer, wearing them across cobblestone New York streets, rainy city commutes, long-distance hikes, and casual weekends around town. In each test, we looked closely at grip, how the soles handled slick surfaces, insulation to keep feet warm in cold weather, and waterproofing to make sure soggy socks weren’t part of the deal. We also rewarded boots that could pull double duty: looking sharp with dress pants or a suit while still holding up for more rugged, off-duty wear.

High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.
  • Sources indicate that chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet.
  • Industry observers note that “High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

Sources indicate that chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

Industry observers note that “High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”.

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the company won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the big bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

“Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”.

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is right now operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

While specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the manufacturer has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The major trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

Mowing milestone: Greenzie surpasses 255,000 autonomous miles mowed

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles.
  • Greenzie revealed the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.
  • And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the organization really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie revealed the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the organization really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

“We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” says Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”.

Greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

“Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” said Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”.

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of significant battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The organization indicates the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.

Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.

Surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong? Or is it?

After Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in October 2024, Brownlee (MKBHD) mentioned there was no way Tesla would deliver a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. If it did, he’d shave his head on camera.

Recent findings suggest that musk has taken it personally ever since. When the first Cybercab came off the Giga Texas line in February, he replied “Gonna happen 😂” to a bald-MKBHD meme, which we covered at the time. In September, after Brownlee doubled down in a newly introduced video, Musk wrote: “I guess he really wants to shave his head 🤷‍♂️”.

In a recent development, on Friday, Tesla started inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use. The order page lists $29,990, a mandatory $299 per month Autonomy Subscription, a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and an estimated delivery of December 2026, only in Tesla’s Texas Robotaxi cities.

It has been revealed that as we reported Friday, the car only operates inside Tesla’s Robotaxi geofences. And Tesla’s Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement states it “will not operate” without the $299 plan, bans owners from putting it on the Robotaxi network or using it for ride-hailing, and lets Tesla shrink the operating area at any time.

So Tesla designed a robotaxi, then offered it to select private owners who aren’t allowed to use it as a taxi. Over five years, that’s $47,631 before insurance, registration, and charging. And you are limited to small geofenced areas. If you stop paying Tesla’s monthly fee, which it can change at all times, your cybercab becomes a paperweight.

In a recent development, brownlee laid out his case Friday night. There are no deliveries yet, the car is invite-only rather than publicly available, and it can’t be used as a cab outside of the existing geofences. He called it “a paperweight if I take this thing home,” though he admits that last point isn’t technically part of the bet.

Industry observers note that the memes are everywhere, so let’s go back over the bet: Cybercab publicly available for under $30k by the end of 2026My hair is safe for several reasons1: No deliveries yet. But they’re estimating starting in December so that’s neat2: Invite only, not actually publicly… https://t.co/NCD2aFbe2c.

Tesla fans fired back with clips from his September video, where he described a car that “will not ship to regular people like you and me for $30k before the end of 2026.” Whole Mars Catalog, an Elon Musk propagandist whose real name is Omar Qazi, told him to “be a man and honor your word.” Musk reposted it, then replied:.

Musk also reposted a Grok answer claiming the current offer “matches” the conditions of the bet.

But around the same time, Musk replied directly to Brownlee’s post about the order page, and it didn’t help Tesla’s case:.

“It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”.

It has been revealed that that’s Tesla’s CEO confirming, a day after launch, that the car can’t be sold outside the areas where it already operates and that its price is wrong. A price that Musk fully controls.

Recent findings suggest that yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a Youtuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We’ve seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single “autonomous delivery” of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

According to recent reports, tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version highlights up that’s invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself says is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it’s a permanent variable rate lease starting at $300 a month with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

Besides, the bet was "under 30k." Starting price is under 30k, but a subscription is required, which takes it over 30k, just to use it for one day. They could have given the car away for free, and just charged a fee to use it. Doesn't change the total cost.

What do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

According to recent reports, you can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms.

This offer simply makes no sense, and Musk is sort of admitting it by saying the price should be the same as FSD, not $300 a month.

Most inversion tables use a simple foam material; the EP-560 ComforTrak backrest is designed to reduce friction and enhance spinal stretch and decompression. We also love that it’s pretty customizable. It comes with built-in tools for easy adjustability, including a Lumbar Bridge for deeper traction on the lower back and Acupressure Nodes that target muscle tension.

It has been revealed that the device is made out of an ultra-durable, heat-treated steel, adding an extra layer of strength and support. If you’re a little closer to the 300-lb range, this is a solid option.

According to recent reports, it’s on the pricier side, but the Harison Electric Inversion Table is a top pick for both Dr. Mesiwala and Dr. Verma thanks to its adjustable footbed, memory-foam backrest, and heavy-duty build. The device is made with seamless welding and a steel frame to support up to 350 pounds, and the ergonomic ankle lock design is supportive without feeling too tight or restrictive. Security is also a top priority, and the table includes a high-quality safety belt that allows you to strap in while inverted (on top of the secure ankle holders).

The table is heavier than other options on this list, but it’s foldable for easy storage. It also includes a 30-day trial and replacement of spare parts within one year for no extra cost.

Read More: The Best Massage Guns, Tested By Us.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for an inversion table that doubles as a massager, here’s your pick. The vertical massage pad covers the entire spine with a contoured lumbar pad for a close-up massage and vibrating sensation, and the in-unit heating pad provides warmth to the lower back. There are also multiple mode settings to suit your massage and heat preferences, and the included user manual provides all necessary instructions and details.

This model has a new, improved ankle-holding system to reduce pressure on the ankles when inverted, while still ensuring a secure, protective fit. There’s also a six-position pin system on the side of the machine that lets you adjust the angle without dismounting the device.

In a recent development, each inversion table accommodates different heights, so it's notable to read the fine print. The Teclor Inversion Table adjusts to fit people up to 6'8", making it a good option for taller people. It also can support up to 350 pounds, one of the largest weight capacities you’ll find.

This is a relatively simple inversion table, and the low price supports that. But you’ll still get a comfortably padded back, cushioned handles, and an easy-to-reach handle for adjustability. The ankle-holding system is thickly padded, too. A double-locking system helps to ensure your device is firmly in place when it’s in use. When you’re done inverting, it folds up small enough to stash in a closet.

Read More: The 6 Best Compression Boots to Support Muscle Recovery.

Sources indicate that consider the Teeter FitSpine LX9 the slightly more luxurious version of our top pick, the X3. This has all the elements users love about the X3, including that durable heat-treated steel frame and padded back, but in a slightly sleeker, user-friendly design. The LX9 has an eight-point floating suspension system for a large range of motion, along with reinforced padded handles for a comfortable grip.

Enjoy eight acupressure nodes to help relieve muscle tension while you hang. The included lumbar bridge is adjustable and works to tweak your hip alignment. The LX9 has a step-through design with a specialized boarding platform to make it easy to get on and off. There’s even a built-in storage caddy to hold your gear while you invert.

It has been revealed that using an inversion table isn’t as simple as diving into a fresh set of dumbbells. These devices require you to move your body upside-down, making it vital to know what you’re doing and how to ease into the process.

Sources indicate that it’s vital to start with a “modest” angle vs. going into a full-out inversion when you’re starting out, according to Raymond Agostino, DPT, owner of Agostino Athletics in Fort Myers, Florida. “The goal is to introduce your body to the position and create a gentle traction effect without overwhelming your system,” he says.

It has been revealed that agostino suggests starting with a gentle recline, like 20 to 25 degrees for 30 to 45 seconds and see how you feel. “If you feel comfortable and don't experience dizziness, increased pain, or other symptoms, you can gradually increase the time or angle over future sessions,” he claims. Agostino recommends only changing one variable at a time—angle and inversion time—to ease yourself in. “You don't need to go farther upside down and stay there longer all at once,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re inverted, you may feel a pressure sensation in your head or a mild “head rush,” Agostino says. “When your head is positioned below your heart, blood pressure and pressure within the eyes can increase, which is one reason inversion feels very different from simply lying flat,” he explains. You might also feel a feeling of fullness in your head or facial pressure. “Those sensations should remain mild and should resolve when you return upright,” according to Agostino.

Agostino points out that you don’t get a trophy for going completely upside down. “If a smaller angle provides the stretch or relief you're looking for, there may be no reason to progress to a full inversion,” he indicates.

Safety is paramount when shopping for an inversion table. "It’s ideal to find a product with comfortable ankle straps and safety locks to keep you secure and in place," says Kushagra Verma, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine surgeon at DISC Sports and Spine Center. You also want to make sure the table can be controlled and manipulated by the user if you strategy to use the device alone. Inversion tables should be used with caution, especially if you’re a beginner, says Rahul Shah, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine and neck surgeon at Premier Orthopaedic Associates. Additionally, older adults and those who have chronic dizziness, high blood pressure, glaucoma, inner ear problems, heart disease, and/or severe injuries should avoid inversion tables without talking to their doctor first, he says. Keep this in mind, too, per Agostino: “A little pressure may be expected. Feeling like something is wrong is not something you need to train yourself to tolerate.” If it feels like your back pain is worsening, or if you develop newly introduced numbness, tingling, weakness, or radiating pain, Agostino recommends that you stop using the inversion tale.

Sturdiness and durability are crucial for preventing accidents or instability while you’re upside down, Dr. Verma claims. He recommends always looking for a product made with high-quality materials, such as stainless steel, to provide better support and longevity. Be sure to read customer reviews and seek expert opinions on the machine's sturdiness when shopping. Of course, all the selections on our list have been vetted in this way.

In addition to safety features, all experts agree that it’s crucial to consider how much weight an inversion table can safely hold. (The machine should clearly state this in the product description.) Because the machine puts you in a rather compromising position, maximum weight capacity is key for keeping you safe and at ease, Dr. Shah claims. Going over the weight capacity raises the odds that the table will break or flip while you’re on it, potentially injuring you in the process, Agostino says.

Industry observers note that it’s vital to consider the table's length to ensure it accommodates your size and height, says Ali Mesiwala, MD, a neurosurgeon and complex spine expert at DISC Sports and Spine Center. Most inversion tables are adjustable for a customized fit, but it’s best to ensure the maximum height is within your range for effective use. The width of the table is another key factor, as a wider table can offer more stability during inversion, particularly if you’re on the taller or heavier side, says Brian Wallace, DC, a chiropractor at Pinewood Family Care. As a general rule of thumb, the width of the table should be wide enough for your core to conformably fit and not fall to either side, Dr. Shah adds.

It has been revealed that depending on your needs, different inversion tables include add-on features like lumbar spine support, heat, memory foam, or massage elements, Dr. Wallace claims. These extra features are not a necessity, but they can be beneficial if you’re looking for added comfort and therapeutic benefits, he says. Just remember: extra add-ons should be considered second to the table's fundamental stability, comfort, and safety.

An inversion table isn’t the cheapest tool you’ll use to reduce your back pain, but there is a range to consider. Most tables will run you anywhere from $150 to $450, with higher-priced models having additional features like heat, memory foam, and massage.

Recent findings suggest that to track down the best inversion tables, Men’s Health editors, including contributor Korin Miller, consulted three orthopedic surgeons, a neurosurgeon, a chiropractor, and two physical therapists to learn more about the crucial features to look for in an inversion table. From there, we looked at the most popular inversion tables on the market and narrowed the field based on our experts’ requirements. Each inversion table was ranked based on factors such as size, weight capacity, and safety features. This story was first published in August, and was updated in November to reflect the most recent products on the market, along with advice on how to use these machines.

Extended inversion can cause excessive blood flow to the head and lead to nausea, vomiting, and dizziness, so Dr. Mesiwala recommends using an inversion table for a maximum of five minutes at a time, up to twice a day. If you’re a beginner, he suggests only inverting for 30 seconds once a day as you get your bearings.

In a recent development, the best time to use an inversion table is typically when your muscles are relaxed, such as after a workout at the end of the day, indicates Dr. Wallace. Remember: You should not be inverted for long periods, and it’s best to start slowly and work your way up to time and frequency.

Recent findings suggest that this is ultimately up to you. Some people feel comfortable with their arms by their sides or crossed over their chest, while others prefer to stretch them overhead. You can also put your arms on the support bars. Essentially, you should do whatever feels comfortable to you.

Recent findings suggest that starting in 2027, Apple TV will become the exclusive U.S. streaming home of F1 Academy, the all-female racing series developing the next generation of talent.

Fans will be able to watch every qualifying session and race on Apple TV, bringing more visibility to a series that is promptly gaining momentum. It also expands Apple's partnership with Formula 1, which began its five-year U.S. broadcast deal with the streaming service in 2026.

For Austrian driver Emma Felbermayr, who represents the Audi Revolut F1 team in F1 Academy, the announcement is particularly exciting.

“Apple TV is such a significant platform, and it's all about F1 Academy getting more attention,” Felbermayr told Women's Health in Las Vegas ahead of the Grand Prix. “It just makes the interest into the sport much bigger, and that's what we need. We need to have more girls interested in the sport so that we get more attention. In the end, we want to get seen by people.".

Recent findings suggest that released in 2022, F1 Academy is a Formula 4-level development series designed to create more opportunities for women in motorsport. And its impact extends beyond the racetrack.

At a private dinner in Las Vegas celebrating the Apple TV announcement, F1 Academy managing director Susie Wolff reflected on the series' rapid rise.

Recent findings suggest that “It's incredible how the sport has shifted in the last five to seven years,” Wolff said. “Women have a huge part to play in that shift, and that has been part of the reason why F1 Academy has had so much success in the short space of time.” The dinner event, co-hosted by Wolff and F1 Chief Commercial Officer Emily Prazer, brought together women from across the worlds of sports, entertainment, and advocacy, including activist Malala Yousafzai and model Kelly Piquet.

According to recent reports, that growth is personal for Felbermayr, who says F1 Academy has helped her become more confident both in and out of the car. Once a self-described shy person, the 19-year-old has learned to navigate interviews, limited track time, and the pressure of competing at a high level.

“I got so much better in the language of English. That's maybe just a small part of it, but just getting more confident in front of the camera, but also in the car,” states Felbermayr, who just signed on for a third F1 Academy season with Audi. “Every challenge grows yourself as a person, and I think that's something I really saw in the last two years.”.

Recent findings suggest that with seven race weekends on the 2027 calendar, including stops in Austin and Las Vegas, American fans will have plenty of opportunities to get acquainted with F1 Academy's rising stars. And with Apple TV bringing their races to a wider audience, more young girls will have the chance to see what's possible behind the wheel.

#132704. What Does Silence Mean in Your Relationships?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (765 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

What Does Silence Mean in Your Relationships?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • I've worked with several couples where the same pattern occurs again and again.
  • Some partners, faced with silence, panic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

I've worked with several couples where the same pattern occurs again and again. They get into a disagreement, and then things escalate until one person goes silent. Silence can have many meanings, but it's not always clear what it means.

Some partners, faced with silence, panic. They don't know what the silence means. They feel shut out and rejected; they escalate and engage more, or they, too, withdraw. But silence isn't universally negative. Silence can be positive, but for many couples, navigating it feels like a minefield that can blow up at any moment.

In a recent development, researchers have identified a few different patterns in relationships that lead to poor outcomes, like the demand-withdraw pattern and the pursue-withdraw pattern (Christensen & Heavey, 1990; Schrodt et al., 2014). These patterns are ultimately unproductive because the concern never really gets resolved, and they generate a lot of conflict. Conflict, by itself, isn't negative per se (Gottman, 1994). Gottman's research reveals that many couples fight, and it isn't destructive if they fight smart and repair any damage done (Gottman & Silver, 1999).

So, let's look at the really harmful form of silence, which comes from the temporal need-threat model (Williams, 2009). He found that the silent treatment threatens four basic needs: belonging, self-esteem, control, and a sense of meaningful existence. Murphy and Hoover (1999) argue that “hostile withdrawal” is a form of emotional abuse. Schrodt et al. (2014) conducted an analysis that included 74 studies of the demand-withdraw pattern, and they found that this pattern predicts lower relationship satisfaction.

Silence can also come from a person feeling overwhelmed. This is what psychologist Gottman (1994) identified as “flooding,” leading to "stonewalling.” It occurs when a person becomes so physiologically aroused that it feels like there are too many inputs at once. The person can't process what's being mentioned or all the emotions it triggers, and so the system overloads and shuts down. One person’s overwhelm can transfer to their partner. Butler et al. (2003) observed that suppressing emotion in conversation increased their partner's blood pressure, so even overwhelmed silence can negatively impact their partner. People who are more avoidant may use "deactivating strategies" (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2016), such as disconnecting from their partner during conflict. In my experience, this can also escalate and intensify conflict because it becomes not just a disagreement, but a threat to the connection.

But as I remarked before, silence isn't always negative; it may occur because one partner wants to process and reflect before continuing the conversation. Kross and Ayduk (2017) found evidence that supports the effectiveness of self-distancing strategies. This involves a person stepping away from a conversation to reduce emotional reactivity and improve reasoning. This is a healthy use of silence. My caveat is that partners should express their need for silence and time to process and reflect, which will help them engage in the conversation more productively. Some people are think-to-talk, and others are talk-to-think. You need to know what kind of person you are and what your needs are, and then be able to explain that to your partner.

Sources indicate that butler, E. A., Egloff, B., Wilhelm, F. H., Smith, N. C., Erickson, E. A., & Gross, J. J. (2003). The social consequences of expressive suppression. Emotion, 3(1), 48–67. https://doi.org/10.1037/1528-3542.3.1.48.

Sources indicate that christensen, A., & Heavey, C. L. (1990). Gender and social structure in the demand/withdraw pattern of marital conflict. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 59(1), 73–81. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.59.1.73.

Industry observers note that gottman, J. M. (1994). What predicts divorce? The relationship between marital processes and marital outcomes. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

Gottman, J. M., & Silver, N. (1999). The seven principles for making marriage work. Crown.

In a recent development, volkswagen revealed how much its new ID. Cross will cost, with prices starting at around $35,000 in the UK. But if you’re hoping to get the cheaper version, you’ll have to wait a bit longer.

Sources indicate that after opening orders for the ID. Cross in Europe in July, Volkswagen is preparing to launch the entry-level electric SUV in the UK.

The ID. Cross is the all-electric equivalent of the T-Cross, Volkswagen’s smallest and most affordable SUV in Europe and the UK.

Industry observers note that following the ID. Polo, the ID. Cross is the latest from Volkswagen’s electric urban family of compact cars.

The electric SUV is 4,153 mm long, about the same length as the T-Cross, but its dedicated MEB+ platform offers more interior space. It seats five and offers a 475-liter boot, 20 liters more than the gas-powered T-Cross with the rear seats pushed all the way forward.

Sources indicate that when the rear seats are folded, the electric ID. Cross offers up to 1,345 liters of overall luggage volume.

Recent findings suggest that like in Europe, the Volkswagen ID. Cross will be available with two battery packs in the UK: a 37 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) pack and a 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) pack.

The ID. Cross with the larger 52 kWh battery offers up to 265 miles of WLTP range, while the 37 kWh version provides up to 194 miles of WLTP range.

With DC fast charging of up to 105 and 88 kW, Volkswagen said the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in as little as 23 minutes.

All versions are equipped with vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities, allowing it to be used as a mobile power bank for an e-bike, campsite, or other external electronic devices.

Inside, the ID. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. The setup includes a 10.25″ Digital Cockpit Pro instrument display and a 12.9″ infotainment screen. Based on driver feedback, Volkswagen brought back physical buttons for climate control and other vehicle functions.

According to recent reports, volkswagen will open orders for the ID. Cross Life and Style trims in the UK with the 52 kWh battery and 208 hp (211 PS) motor will go on sale on Thursday, November 19, starting at £30,260 ($40,000) and £33,675 ($44,500), respectively.

The base ID. Cross Life and Style trims with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, with prices starting at £26,985 ($35,500) and £30,400 ($40,100).

It has been revealed that volkswagen noted the 52 kWh version is eligible for the UK government’s £1,500 ($2,000) electric car grant. Eligibility for the 37 kWh versions is expected to be confirmed soon.

In Europe, Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000) in Germany, including VAT.

It has been revealed that as the electric counterpart to its popular T-Cross, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer noted the ID. Cross is “modern, reliable, and above all, affordable.”.

According to recent reports, sadly, VW has no plans to bring the ID. Cross to the US. In early 2027, it will launch the latest ID. Tiguan, which will replace the outgoing ID.4 SUV.

#132702. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1512 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help.
  • Recent findings suggest that police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system.
  • Sources indicate that just before 4 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

Recent findings suggest that police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Sources indicate that just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

It has been revealed that then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report says the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

Sources indicate that A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson said the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”.

Sources indicate that so that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody said a word about Autopilot.

It has been revealed that under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

According to recent reports, it identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and notes it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

The report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

It has been revealed that how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

Recent findings suggest that A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a major truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In a recent development, in 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

It has been revealed that trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a massive, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

We want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

The NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a new monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

Sources indicate that september may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash shows how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Recent findings suggest that three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

That's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Industry observers note that compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

According to recent reports, tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

Either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

In a recent development, we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

This is part of the Men's Health Body Bible, a collection of cutting-edge stories focused on helping you build more muscle using the latest science and lessons from some of the finest athletes and trainers on the planet.

THE SECRET TO training your abs is out—and it entails more than situps and planks, more than just targeting your rectus abdominis, the ballyhooed band of muscle between your chest and your hips. If you want true core strength (and, yes, that six-pack), a growing group of experts will tell you that you need to carry heavy weights and walk. This forces your core to constantly microcorrect and rebalance as you move, explains Aaron Horschig, C.S.C.S., D.P.T., a St. Louis–based physical therapist. You also need to twist and turn, challenging your oblique muscles and back extensors.

It has been revealed that “While there’s nothing wrong with training the abs for show, training for stability—which encompasses all of the muscles that surround the spine and hips—is essential training for everyone,” says Horschig. His new book, Rebuilding Milo, includes a variety of exercises, many of which challenge your entire core—think lower back extensors, glutes, and obliques, which all team up with your abs to stabilize and bolster your back, lending postural support.

Unlike body parts that handle just one or two tasks (like your biceps, which are most heavily utilized to bend your elbows), all those core muscles have a host of responsibilities. They work together to flex your spine (as happens during a classic situp), and they help rotate your shoulders so you can turn to look at a friend. They also prevent excessive rounding of the lower back (known as anti-flexion), a key tactic in the battle to stop back pain. The ideal abs regimen trains all these functions, protecting you against injuries and readying your core (and spine) for anything life can throw at you. Horschig says people finally get that. “More and more people are starting to understand the true role of core,” he says.

According to recent reports, the end result of all this work? A lower back that’s armor-plated against persistent pain, and the ability to move athletically and fluidly. And along the way, you’ll build those six-pack abs, too.

It has been revealed that HOW TO DO IT:An underrated plank upgrade, this move challenges your abs and obliques (and your glutes, too!). Start in pushup position, feet wide. Lift your left hand and touch it to your right shoulder. Keep your hips square as you do. Repeat on the other side.

REPS & SETS:Work for time, not reps, doing three 40-second sets.

In a recent development, HOW TO DO IT:Stand in a split stance, left shoulder next to the high pulley of a cable machine, both hands grasping the handle, then bend at the knees until your left thigh is nearly parallel to the floor. Keep your hips square to the front as you pull the cable across your body, then return it to the start.

REPS & SETS:Do 10 to 12 reps per side. Do 3 sets.

Recent findings suggest that HOW TO DO IT:Stand holding kettlebells in both hands, the left bell at your chest, the right bell at your hip. Walk forward (or march in place) for 10 to 15 steps per leg. Move slowly, working to keep your hips square.

REPS & SETS:Do 2 sets per side, challenging your abs and lower-back muscles to keep you upright against the heavy load.

Recent findings suggest that TRAIN YOUR ABS EVERYDAY. Some muscle groups require several days to recover, but your core muscles are built to be resilient. That means you can train them nearly every day. Consider doing 3 or 4 sets of core work in every work- out, rotating in fresh and different ab exercises to continually challenge your rectus abdominis, oblique muscles, and lower-back spinal erectors.

Recent findings suggest that NEVER GOING HEAVY. Bodyweight planks and situps are a solid starting point for your ab training. But just like any other muscle, core muscles are meant to be loaded and overloaded. Add resistance to your core training, and don’t be afraid to challenge yourself, especially on moves like the mixed-rack carry above. “You have to do that sometimes,” indicates the popular bodybuilder and trainer known as Ulisses Jr. “I’d be lying if I told you I didn’t load my abs.”.

The crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

It has been revealed that late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

According to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly mentioned which.

Mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

In a recent development, CHP indicates the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

In a recent development, under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

The rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police noted it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

Recent findings suggest that how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

Industry observers note that two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

It has been revealed that CHP hasn’t mentioned whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing new rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

#132698. What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Phys ↗ Open Full Page

What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (82 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Phys

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

We usually picture mountain building as rock being pushed upward. But deep beneath some mountain belts and volcanic arcs, the opposite can happen: dense rock at the base of the crust can become unstable, break away and sink hundreds of kilometers into the mantle, dragging part of the rigid outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) with it. Seismic images suggest that this process, known as lithospheric dripping, has occurred beneath the central Andes and California's Sierra Nevada.
